in writing. ‒ i am firmly opposed to the report by the committee on the internal market. for the most part, the statements on the implementation of the eu single market rules in the eea countries (iceland, liechtenstein and norway) are quite consistent. what i cannot accept, however, are the very critical references to switzerland because of the 2014 referendum against mass immigration and the subsequent decisions of the swiss federal council. legitimate, albeit just, decisions taken by the swiss people and the swiss government have nothing to do with the internal market of the union in the movement of goods. the schwab report is undoubtedly an illegal interference in the choices of the swiss people.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the report on the agreement between the european economic area (eea) and switzerland, which is a valuable incentive for economic growth and an optimal instrument for extending the single market to third countries and ensuring the soundness of the single market also in the long term. in may 2014, new negotiations were launched to outline an institutional framework essential for concluding further agreements on switzerland's participation in the internal market, although some issues remain, such as the recent swiss restriction on the free movement of persons or obstacles to cross-border professional mobility, which can create a strong imbalance and significantly undermine the benefits of the agreements for eu member states. as the report points out, our relations with switzerland must therefore be further developed to mutual advantage and to the benefit of the many common points already in existence.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the european economic area - switzerland: obstacles to the full implementation of the internal market because a well-functioning single market, based on a social market economy, is necessary to stimulate our growth.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal under consideration on the obstacles to the full implementation of the internal market in the eea-switzerland countries. in particular, while noting the outcome of the february 2014 referendum against 'mass immigration' and the decisions taken by the swiss federal council, the proposal notes that these decisions are contrary to the obligations under the agreement on the free movement of persons and therefore calls on switzerland to respect those obligations; deplores the unilateral accompanying measures and calls on the confederation to remove obstacles to cross-border professional mobility in order to intensify the internal market.
in writing. ‒ switzerland's choice to remain outside the eu is legitimate, even if i do not agree with it. however, such a small country, although strong in some specific areas, cannot help but share some policies with the surrounding giants: i am referring in particular to the internal market and free movement. that said, i believe that the eu must monitor and enforce the respect of the four freedoms, in particular the freedom of movement of workers, so that all parties benefit from the benefits of the agreements. i am referring, if it is not clear, to italian crossborder workers who are subject to unacceptable harassment and discrimination, and against whom we should fight with special information campaigns on behalf of the confederation. i voted in favour of the general structure of the report and the appropriate emphasis on this aspect, and i congratulate the rapporteur on the excellent work he has done.
in writing. ‒ this is a very important own-initiative report which i supported by voting in favour of it. the european union has a free trade association (efta) with some non-eu countries, such as iceland, liechtenstein, norway and switzerland, including the economic free trade area (efta) agreement. however, there is a serious shortfall in the transposition of european legislation on the single market by these states. the backlog of legal acts awaiting incorporation is still too high and efforts must be made to ensure that they are transposed in a timely manner in compliance with the agreements, with due regard for reciprocity and fairness. i also share the disappointment at the outcome of the popular initiative against mass immigration in switzerland on 9 february 2014 and the decisions taken by the federal council on a draft implementing law and new accompanying measures. it is essential to respect european law and to remove immediately the obstacles to cross-border professional mobility in order to intensify the internal market.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report by mr schwab, which provides a significant overview of the state of implementation of single market legislation between the countries of the european economic area (eea) and the swiss confederation. the eea agreement, if properly applied, can make a major contribution to the eu's economic growth and i hope that non-eu countries will also transpose and effectively implement single market legislation. the report also deals in a balanced way with the state of bilateral relations with the swiss confederation, which are now based only on a number of bilateral agreements. i hope that switzerland will be able to fully respect the commitments it has made to the eu in these agreements, in particular on the free movement of persons (the ftap agreement), and that it will review the provisions restricting the free movement of workers and the mobility of students. more recently, two regulations adopted by the canton of ticino have affected italian crossborder workers. i believe that these are clearly discriminatory measures against european citizens, in clear breach of the provisions of the ftaa. the european union will not accept any restrictions on the freedom of establishment and the free movement of persons, which is the founding principle of the single market.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on migration and refugees in europe, because the very founding principles of the european union and its identity are at stake in these issues. the humanitarian disaster has been raging for months, from the shores of lampedusa to the train station in budapest, from the calais railway lines to the macedonian railway barriers. it is therefore time for our europe to take a step backwards, even if it is by self-criticism of the inertia of the past few months. we must now build a new common policy based on a sense of responsibility, solidarity and mutual respect. we must recover a european ideal, which does not mean welcoming everyone indiscriminately, which would be an impossible task, but it means trying to save those who are fleeing from conflicts and war zones, which is a duty for us europeans. the leaders of the eu and its member states have an obligation to take a clear stand for respect for human dignity and the rights of asylum seekers, demonstrating that the union is not only based on economic directives and the internal market but also and above all on solidarity.

in writing. ‒ forced labour is a crime that is unfortunately still present today, with tens of thousands of people falling victim to human traffickers every year. the international labour organization (ilo) estimated that some 21 million people were working in slavery in 2014. although the international convention against forced labour was signed in 1930, action against traffickers is still lacking and discontinuous, with particular shortcomings in the cooperation of criminal prosecution between states. effective measures are needed for the identification, release, protection, recovery and assistance of victims of forced labour. the ilo states parties are required to ensure that all victims have access to remedies (such as compensation) and that the competent authorities are authorised not to prosecute victims for illegal activities which they have been forced to commit against their will. the european parliament must therefore ratify the 2014 protocol on the protection of victims of trafficking as soon as possible, and recommend that the member states ratify it as soon as possible in order to finally put an end to a phenomenon that is, in all respects, a disgrace to humanity.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the text to authorise member states to ratify the 2014 protocol to the 1930 forced labour convention, which strengthens the prevention of trafficking in human beings for the purpose of exploitation and ensures the protection and compensation of victims of forced labour. among the most important provisions is the obligation for states to develop a national action plan to combat forced labour effectively, by taking measures to ensure that legislation on the prevention of forced labour applies to all workers and in every sector of the economy. in particular, the rules aim to protect people, especially migrant workers, from potentially abusive and fraudulent recruitment and placement practices, thereby addressing the root causes of forced labour risks. this protocol is therefore intended to safeguard fundamental rights and to strengthen the fight against trafficking in human beings. its ratification is a major step forward in the fight against criminal organizations throughout europe, and that is why i have decided to vote in favour of the text.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i consider this measure which we have voted for today to be extremely important. i hope that the commission will act promptly and tenaciously to define an even more organic measure. i believe that this is something that links in particular italian history, a centuries-old history, to european manufacturing and therefore protection by geographical indication is going to make our small and medium-sized enterprises even more competitive as they face an increasingly global market which must have the quality assurance that italian enterprises attach to their products.
in writing. ‒ the possible extension of the protection of the typical geographical indications of the european union to non-agricultural products is a major step forward for the protection of traditional european high-quality products. protection is based on the need to preserve products which are the result of traditional knowledge and techniques and are characteristic of entire european regions. excellent products are constantly the victims of counterfeiting and fraud. in order to curb these phenomena, which are detrimental to both consumers and producers, i believe it is necessary to create a protected geographical indication, also for non-agricultural products, so as to provide adequate protection for both parties. european harmonisation is needed as some states do not offer specific protection while in others definitions and procedures are visible. in italy, for example, there is no such protection. in this connection i believe that a harmonized procedure should be completely free of charge without adding any additional burden to the undertakings. we have fought for this and we will continue to watch. for these reasons, my vote was in favour.

in writing. ‒ the european union has a rich range of quality non-agricultural products, which reflect the diversity of local characteristics, often handmade, and which constitute an immense cultural and economic heritage not only for the country of origin but for the union as a whole. the geographical indication (gi), currently reserved for products of agricultural origin, has helped to enhance the position of these products on international markets as they are considered safe and of high quality by consumers. the lack of a harmonised and consistent system of protection of gi for non-agricultural products at european level has so far undermined the eu's ability to negotiate trade agreements with third countries which, on the other hand, provide for all gi for non-agricultural products in their legislation. the possibility of extending gi's to non-agricultural products in europe, in addition to protecting our traditional productions, would strengthen the eu's negotiating capacity both bilaterally and multilaterally in the wto. for these reasons i voted in favour of the report and i join the call on the european commission to consider and submit legislative proposals as soon as possible for a uniform protection of european gi for non-agricultural products.

author of the book. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we are talking about a sad story today. it is a very sad story, because in recent years we thought that we had made a real and practical contribution to reducing emissions from the car industry, and that we had achieved important goals so that european citizens could live in a cleaner environment. in reality, we are faced with something very different, because we have not been able to guarantee citizens a better air to breathe. we are now certain that our desire to legislate was only an illusion, an illusion based on fraud that we were unable to prevent or detect. it is therefore clear that we now know that the limits for nitrogen monoxide emissions have been deliberately exceeded for many years by one of the largest and most powerful car manufacturers. as chairman of the envi committee i am therefore concerned, as are the colleagues who will speak after me, and i ask the european commission whether there were other pollutants involved, such as particulate matter, carbon monoxide or others, or whether we are talking only about nitrogen monoxide, given the great link between these pollutants. is it true, as we have read in some press reports, that emissions were more than 40 times higher than the permitted limits? we want to know the truth and so i ask the european commission to carry out the necessary investigations and above all to keep the european parliament constantly informed of the results of the investigations. we thank the commission for being willing to come to the environment committee, to report immediately after the discovery of the scandal, but we would also like to know whether it is true, as stated by many car manufacturers besides volkswagen, that they did not manipulate car emissions tests. we therefore ask the commission to ensure that these are also subject to independent scrutiny, because what is at stake is very important, since it is the health of european citizens that is at stake. mr president, what has happened is a sad story for another reason. i am referring here to the role of the type-approval authorities. how is it that these authorities have not discovered the existence of illegal mechanisms in such a long period of time? how are these tests carried out and with what tools and equipment? as we all know, it was an american university that discovered this fraud, but we should also ask the member states, those responsible for the controls, those responsible for these technical bodies, how is it possible that these cars have passed the type approval tests? what is the european commission's role in this area and what does commissioner bieńkowska think about the possible establishment of a type approval or surveillance authority which would of course be able to monitor the control and verification operations carried out in the individual member states? i am also thinking of the local authorities and cities which are currently failing to meet the required air quality standards and have already been the subject of infringement proceedings by the european commission, at least they now know what was going on. there was someone who didn't follow the rules and they were held, perhaps wrongly, unfairly responsible. mr president, commissioner bieńkowska, we have therefore discovered in the last few days that the actual nitrogen monoxide emissions of some diesel vehicles measured on the road may indeed be different and divergent from those calculated in the laboratory and for this reason the commission is developing new methods of measuring these emissions, the so-called real drive emission, based on the use of the car in normal driving conditions. with regard to this new testing methodology from 2017, i would like to ask whether the commission can clarify whether it will be based on conformity factors or on a sample test. in conclusion, i hope that this scandal will help to find out what is really going on in this sector and whether we are dealing with an isolated case or with a common wrongdoing by several companies. i wonder why the european union always has to wait for scandal or tragedy to act. it's happened before in the food industry, with bse to get traceability of meat. what happened was that we needed to have thousands of deaths in the mediterranean to respond with a european policy and an agenda on migration. we are now facing a scandal, did it take this scandal to make you realize that the system needed to change and had to be set up differently?

president-in-office of the council.– mr president, honourable members, thank you for this very important and very crucial question because the abolition of the death penalty lies at the heart of our european values. no state should have a right to decide on the life and death of its citizens. we all believe that, and i am quoting, ‘a just and necessary punishment must never exclude the dimension of hope and the goal of rehabilitation’. these are the words pronounced by pope francis in front of the us congress recently. since 1983, the ‘no’ to capital punishment is part of the acquis communautaire, it is part of who we are. it is, then, an honour to address this plenary debate only days away from 10 october, the 13th world and europe day against the death penalty. the end of the death penalty is something that is worth fighting for. let us not forget our own history. still in the 1970s executions took place in western europe and i remember that in one of the big countries a socialist president abolished the death penalty in 1982. behind the iron curtain executions took place till the late 1980s but today the european union is 100% free from capital punishment. things can change. we can and must be a force for this change. so we have to be clear on one thing: never be afraid to raise the issue of abolition as part of our external action. it must be a cornerstone of our own european foreign policy. ten years ago only 59 countries had fully abolished the death penalty. now there are 101 of us. ten years ago, 41 countries carried out executions. in 2014 the number went down to 22, a lot less, although still too many. many countries have ended capital punishments in practice. others have taken steps to narrow the scope of the death penalty. today 140 countries are abolitionist in law or in practice. however, the grim side of the statistics is that still in 2015 thousands of people were executed or sentenced to death and thousands of people are on death row worldwide. and the number of death sentences went up between 2013 and 2014, a scary statistic. you mentioned it in your presentation. the abolition of the death penalty worldwide requires all our best energies, all our political commitment. the use of the death penalty for drug offences is a very emblematic and cruel aspect of death penalty use. the international human rights law is clear: drug crimes do not constitute most serious crimes for which capital punishment may be prescribed. unfortunately, many asian countries still retain the death penalty for those crimes, including as a mandatory form of punishment. in iran at least 75% out of this year’s 660 executions have been related to drug crimes. on a smaller but still significant scale, the same happens in saudi arabia and other countries. but this is not the only worrying trend. the death penalty is still applied for crimes which again fall outside the category of most serious ones. this includes economic crimes, apostasy, adultery or even sexual relationships between consenting adults. furthermore, despite explicit international law provisions, some countries sentence and even execute minors and mentally disabled persons. we also cannot ignore the fact that many death sentences are the products of unfair trials, often without appeals, guarantee or clemency procedures. some countries resort to the cruellest of execution methods such as public beheadings or crucifixions, and many refuse to notify the families of death row inmates prior to executions. let there be no doubt the eu is a leading actor in the abolitionist cause. abolition is embodied in strong, rigorous and effective eu guidelines on the matter. the fight against the death penalty features as a top priority in the new action plan on human rights and democracy which we adopted last july. throughout 2015 the eu has used all diplomatic tools to advance the cause of worldwide abolition. we condemn the continuing extensive use of the death penalty in parts of the world some of which are at our doorstep. iran, iraq, saudi arabia, pakistan, indonesia, belarus, egypt, japan, singapore, china, vietnam and the united states of america were a particular focus of attention. more than 30 statements were issued and demarches were carried out in many other countries, based on the minimum standards defined by international law and the eu guidelines on that penalty. we have been the most vocal advocate of abolition worldwide. still, i know some of you believe the eu has not always been as loud as it should be. let me be frank: condemnation is important but it is often not enough. ultimately, i believe there is no alternative to engagement with those who do not share our views and values. this is the most effective contribution we can give to the cause of abolition. for this reason, we are intensifying our dialogue with the most fervent retentionist countries at all levels. we are constantly stepping up efforts, especially in countries where there is a spike in executions or the reintroduction of capital punishment, sometimes after decades of moratorium. our individual human rights country strategies have identified the abolition of the death penalty as a top priority in all retentionist countries. our political or dedicated human rights dialogues constantly feature the issue on their agendas, even when we meet with like-minded countries such as the united states or japan. let me assure you that the question of the death penalty is raised with all interlocutors concerned, beyond any strategic considerations. we are talking to our counterparts in pakistan, iran, saudi arabia and also other countries, and we make it clear that the death penalty is not a remedy to terrorism or criminality, or a question of justice for the victim’s family. we will keep on this double track: challenge and engage. bilateral relations are not the only forum for raising this kind of issue. we are also exploring our regional connections. for example, we are conscious that africa represents the biggest concentration of countries which are abolitionist in practice, and it could potentially become the next death-free continent after europe. this is why the eu actively supported the recent steps taken by the african union towards the adoption of an additional protocol to the african charter on human and peoples’ rights on the abolition of the death penalty. we are currently planning a regional campaign on the asian continent with the aim of animating the public debate on the question of the right to life and human dignity. on an even bigger stage, the eu has worked extensively on the united nations general assembly resolution on a moratorium on executions. i am proud to say that, thanks to the eu’s extensive lobbying and support, the moratorium was adopted in december 2014 with an unprecedented number of 117 votes in favour and a record number of 95 co-sponsors. the eu can be a beacon for abolitionists worldwide but we need to build partnerships on a global scale to succeed, and our success on the moratorium tells us something; we are not alone in this fight. mr president, i would like to take the opportunity to express my gratitude for the european parliament’s constant and fervent dedication to the abolitionist cause. this is reflected in numerous resolutions and dedicated debates but also in missions in third countries where honourable members do not shy away from raising the issue of executions, even with the most difficult interlocutors. we can count on a global network of partners advancing human dignity, and the global moratorium on the death penalty is at the core of our foreign policy. this is about the foundations and the fundamental values of europe, and we will keep engaging with our partners on this issue for a world where no state can dispose of the life of its citizens.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the death penalty is the most cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, it violates the right to life and, whatever form it takes, it remains a violent punishment that has no place in today's criminal justice system. in many countries governments justify the use of the death penalty by claiming that it is a deterrent to violent crime, makes society safer, reduces drug-related crime, is enforceable because it is supported by the majority of public opinion, and provides the best cost-effective solution to violent crime. many argue that abolition of the death penalty causes a higher crime rate, but studies in canada, for example, refute this theory. in 2003, 27 years after the abolition of the death penalty, the murder rate in canada had dropped by 44 percent. far from making society safer, the death penalty has proven to have a brutalizing effect on society, being the ultimate sanction a state can inflict on a person, only serving to condone the use of force and to persist in the cycle of violence. once criminals are aware that they have committed a capital crime, they have no interest in reducing their potential, or committing new murders or crimes. if, for example, armed robbery carries the death penalty, the robber has nothing to lose by killing any witnesses during his escape attempt. at the same time, it should be remembered that the use of the death penalty for drug-related offences is a violation of international law. countries that execute people for drug-related offences include indonesia, saudi arabia, china, iran, malaysia and singapore, and there is no clear evidence that the use of the death penalty for these offences acts as a more effective deterrent than long-term imprisonment. i believe that politics must assert its leadership by putting human rights first, opposing the death penalty and explaining to its voters why these actions cannot be taken by a state. amnesty international research shows that public support for the death penalty is based primarily on the desire to be free from crime. and here again, polls conducted in the united states, for example, say that support for the death penalty dropped from 65 percent to 48 percent when life imprisonment was proposed as an option. finally, society cannot accept violence and the sacrifice of human rights as a cost-saving measure. the decision to take a human life should not be based on economic considerations . using the death penalty to reduce the prison population is a futile argument. the united states, for example, has a prison population of two and a half million people, of which 3,000 are on death row, and if they were all convicted and killed, it would not change anything about the prison population. the european union must take decisive action to abolish the death penalty everywhere.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it seems clear to me that the death penalty is the most degrading, the highest violation of human rights. i agree with what the chairman of the subcommittee on human rights, mr valenciano, said in the opening remarks. now, here's the thing. i'd make a little reasoning. we are accustomed to thinking, here in europe, that the death penalty is something medieval, something ancient. we're assuming that it doesn't exist anymore. we have a great deal of trade with countries where the death penalty is on the agenda, and i would like to refer in particular to what we consider to be our closest, not to say our friendliest, country, from which we have received the most influence, namely the united states of america, from which we have taken economic policy, from which we take influence in all respects. i am not saying that the death penalty is a crime, but i am saying that it is a crime, and i am not saying that it is a crime, but i am saying that it is a crime, and i am not saying that it is a crime. this should make us think.

member of the commission.– madam president, i am pleased to participate in this debate on behalf of my colleague, commissioner vella, who unfortunately cannot be here this evening. the directive to reduce pollution from medium combustion installations is a key component of the commission’s clean air policy package presented in december 2013. it is an important deliverable for the 7th environmental action programme, which would help to reduce significantly the potential risks to human health, a programme that i am very familiar with, which was adopted during the irish presidency in 2013. air pollution degrades our environment and it remains the number one environmental cause of death in the eu. it causes 400 000 premature deaths and more than 100 000 lost working days in the eu each year. the medium combustion plants directive will close an unacceptable gap in our legislation and will thus make an important contribution to reaching the future reduction targets as proposed in the amendment to the national emission ceilings directive that is still on the table for the co-legislators. on behalf of my colleague, commissioner vella, let me thank and congratulate the rapporteur, mr grzyb, and his colleagues from the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi) for their commitment and hard work on this proposal. thanks to the work of the parliament negotiating team, it has been possible to maintain the environmental integrity of the proposed directive, whilst addressing justified cases where member states needed flexibility for implementation. the flexibility provisions that cover district heating and the use of biomass as a fuel, which are two major issues for parliament, will ensure that climate and air quality policies are consistent and their synergies are maximised. parliament also made clear that certain further issues are important, such as energy efficiency and carbon monoxide emissions. the commission will address these under the agreed review clauses. allow me also to point out that the medium combustion plants directive is a good example of better regulation. it has been designed to be affordable for smes and it provides long-term certainty for all economic operators concerned, while minimising the administrative burden for both industry and member states. finally, i would like to underline that, beyond being environmentally efficient, this directive promotes advanced eu technology. it will encourage continued innovation and help eu industry gain shares of the rapidly growing global market in pollution control technology. the commission thus fully supports the compromise, although i have to make a declaration on the use of the no-opinion clause for the adoption of implementing acts.
on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner hogan, i would first of all like to thank rapporteur grzyb and all the colleagues who have worked hard to achieve this agreement which allows us to have european legislation and emission limits for a sector which until now was unregulated. i also thank the commissioner and the presidency for the spirit of cooperation they have shown throughout the whole process of the proposal. the proposal, as the rapporteur has pointed out, concerns medium combustion plants, 150 000 plants in europe with a rated thermal output of between 1 and 50 megawatts, and is designed to make a significant contribution to reducing pollution by setting limit values for existing and new plants and also by establishing a registration system which can enable member states to comply with their emission reduction obligations. the aim, of course, is to preserve air quality and thus the health of citizens from possible factors of increasing air pollution. the text represents a compromise between the different positions, but in general an agreement was reached which partly amended the commission's proposal, improving the possibilities of realistically implementing the directive, allowing it to achieve the objective of improving air quality in the european union, without, however, imposing excessive burdens on companies. among the most important points are the obligation for member states to assess the need to apply stricter emission limit values in areas not complying with union air quality standards and the inclusion of a review clause to verify progress in 2020 in terms of energy efficiency of combustion plants. these efforts are part of the wider preparations for cop21 in paris, to confirm the european union as the main actor in the fight against climate change, and we hope that an ambitious agreement will be reached, also thanks to the commitment of all parties involved.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the european union. we are finally filling a glaring regulatory gap, over 142 000 firms with combustion plants between 1 and 50 megawatts were lacking clear regulation. we are talking about plants for the production of electricity, for heating, for cooling, for the production of steam in industrial processes. we're talking about sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, particulate matter. this is what we're talking about. an important step forward in tackling air pollution more effectively. we will never forget it - the commissioner said earlier - the leading cause of death in europe - one of the main causes of eutrophication, with 62% of the european union's surface at risk. that is not all that we as a group of socialists and democrats would have wanted. it is certainly a step forward, a reasonable agreement that protects our health and that of the planet, without harming european businesses. we have made clear choices, i recall a few, we have extended the scope of monitoring to include carbon monoxide, we have reached a reasonable compromise on emission limit values on implementation times, the obligation for member states to assess the need for stricter measures for areas above the limits for air quality, reduction of derogations and then a compromise on a slightly longer implementation times for plants that are part of biomass-fired heating networks. it is for all these reasons that tomorrow we as a group of socialists and democrats will support this measure with conviction.
on behalf of the efdd group. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the directive is implemented. the amendments made by parliament have even weakened the commission's proposal, but above all they have excluded offshore oil platforms and biomass-fired plants from the legislation, which can thus pollute without limits, and if we are talking about employment, the real competitiveness of companies lies in their capacity for ecological innovation and therefore in the use of new sources of clean and free energy, and instead, with the usual excuse that this is better than nothing, we are paying yet another bribe to the power plant industry and the oil multinationals.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to express my full support for this very important measure. firstly, as already mentioned, a legislative gap is being filled, since medium combustion plants up to 50 megawatts are not regulated at european level, although they account for 80% of the total, are used for a very large number of applications and produce about a third of the emissions of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and polluting particles. air pollution has a major impact on the health of citizens and on the costs of national health systems. the final text is a good result, thanks also to the work done by the rapporteur - to whom i am grateful - by our shadow rapporteur, mr massimo paolucci, and by the minister for the environment, mr galletti, during the italian presidency. a bold proposal which, applied gradually to both new and existing plants, is intended to make a significant contribution to reducing pollution, without, however, imposing an excessive burden on our undertakings.
the reporter. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, in march 2014 the european commission presented the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to casein and caseinates intended for human consumption and repealing council directive 83/417/eec, on the basis of article 114 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. tomorrow's vote is essentially a vote on a technical matter, but it has consequences for citizens and consumers, and i have therefore worked on this proposal very carefully, together with my shadow rapporteurs, whom i thank for the excellent cooperation that has enabled us to reach a final agreement with the council in a very short time. we have generally welcomed the commission's proposal and have considered it appropriate to amend certain aspects of it. the commission proposal provides for the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to certain milk proteins intended for human consumption. however, several changes have occurred since the entry into force of the directive, in particular the development of a broad regulatory framework in the food sector and the adoption of an international codex alimentarius regulation on casein-based food products. the production of milk casein and milk caseinates was subject to a subsidy scheme within the union until 2006. the scheme was therefore terminated and was subsequently definitively repealed by the 2013 political agreement on the reform of the single common organisation of the market in agricultural products. on 24 february 2015, the envi committee adopted six amendments to the commission proposal and we worked to lay the foundations for offering food business operators equal treatment on the world market, taking into account the adaptation of the composition requirements for food caseins and caseinates defined in the annexes to the codex alimentarius standard. in particular, the proposal aims to align the powers conferred on the commission with the distinction between delegated and implementing acts introduced by the treaty on the functioning of the union, to update the provisions applicable to caseins and caseinates, taking into account eu legislation adopted in the meantime, in particular that applicable to foodstuffs, and to bring the compositional requirements for caseins into line with the international standard. following agreement with the council, the final text provides for the maximum moisture content of casein to be fixed at 12%, compared with 10% previously, and the maximum fat content of casein milk at 2% compared with 2.25%. this will allow for a rapid future adaptation to international standards and technical progress. although the products covered by the proposal are not intended for direct sale to the final consumer but for sale between food preparation businesses, it is important that food business operators have the necessary data for the labelling of finished products, in particular as regards allergens. the proposal therefore includes provisions on the labelling of caseins and caseinates intended for human consumption, so that their presence is indicated visibly, legibly and indelibly. if the required information is not provided on packaging, containers or labels, the products concerned may not be marketed or used for the preparation of foodstuffs. it is clear that this will enable final consumers to make informed choices, particularly in the case of food allergies and intolerances, and this confirms once again our action to protect european consumers and their health. with tomorrow's vote, europe has put a great deal of emphasis on food issues, with a particular focus on food security, which is always at the heart of our political agenda.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the measure under consideration concerning the limitation of emissions of certain pollutants into the atmosphere. there are around 150 000 medium combustion plants (thermal capacity between 1 and 50 mw) in the eu, used for a wide range of applications (including electricity generation or domestic heating/cooling), producing emissions of pollutants such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and dust. medium-sized plants are the only ones which have not yet been regulated at european level. the commission proposal aims to significantly reduce pollution from nox, so2 and dust by setting limit values and establishing a registration system, to make a significant contribution to the member states' emission reduction obligations.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because air pollutant emissions from combustion plants are generally not regulated at european level. the commission proposal therefore contains forward-looking provisions for these plants. in addition, the report, with its various amendments, is designed to reduce pollution in an indicative way by setting limit values for new and existing installations, together with a simple registration system, in order to help deliver a significant part of the emission reduction obligations and to avoid possible trade-offs between air quality and biomass increase. finally, the emission limit values have been amended in accordance with the laws in force and the principle of cost efficiency will be introduced, with a new distinction between categories of plants on the basis of their nominal heat output. one of the european union's main objectives is to safeguard the lives and health of its citizens, starting with the protection of air quality.
in writing. ‒ i support the proposal for a directive put forward by the european commission and the council on the limitation of atmospheric pollutants by medium combustion plants. although european legislation regulates emissions from small and large plants, there is no regulation for medium-sized plants. the aim of the proposal for a directive is to reduce pollution and dust by setting maximum values for existing and new medium-sized plants. in addition, it provides for the establishment of a system of registration of installations to be applied within the member states which does not impose an excessive administrative burden on undertakings, for example by avoiding double regulation of emissions and instead creating a simple and coherent regulatory environment. i voted in favour of the report because this directive would be an important instrument for improving environmental conditions, quality of life, health costs and european development in the context of the climate and energy challenges. however, there must be a balance between the costs for companies to monitor emissions and the environmental and health benefits. only by adopting proportionate and workable parameters can the cross-border problem of air pollution be tackled effectively.
in writing. ‒ air pollution has caused and continues to cause irreversible damage to the environment and human health across europe. the who estimated the cost of this to be 1.4 trillion, equivalent to one tenth of the eu's gdp in the year 2013. in particular, medium combustion plants (mfus) contribute significantly to poor air quality as sources of emissions of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter. since these plants have not been regulated at eu level, the commission has proposed to take measures against the emission of air pollutants from combustion plants with a rated thermal input between 1 and 50 mw. the definition of the emission limit value (elv) means not only trying to solve the problem at its root, but also contributing to the creation of new jobs by making the companies concerned competitive. i am voting against this because the project is not ambitious enough in view of the technological innovations already in place which could tackle the problem at its root more effectively. i also do not think it is right to exclude certain plants from the scope of the directive, such as hydrogen sulphide conversion plants.
in writing. ‒ although emissions of pollutants from combustion in medium-sized plants are increasingly contributing to pollution, these emissions were not comprehensively regulated by european legislation. i therefore voted in favour of the report because it fills a serious legislative gap. the directive will also help to improve air quality, promote energy efficiency and modernise industrial plants, thereby reducing the negative impact on human health and improving the quality of the environment.
in writing. ‒ setting emission limit values (elvs) would be an effective way to solve europe's air pollution problems by addressing the problem at source, making the environment cleaner, citizens less exposed and avoiding huge socioeconomic costs for europe. the lei could also create competitiveness for the companies concerned and increase eco-innovation, thereby contributing to job creation in europe. as the five star movement we do not support the proposal because of the lack of ambition shown in reducing the limit values for vle emissions and because of the fact that we have not included highly toxic pollutants such as mercury, dioxins and furans in the calculation of the emissions we have proposed. we are concerned about the amendments which have weakened the commission's proposal, the longer time taken to comply with the elvs and the exclusion of certain plants from the scope of the directive.
in writing. ‒ according to european commission estimates, air pollution causes over 400 000 premature deaths every year and costs healthcare up to eur 940 billion. it also contributes to severe environmental degradation and causes economic damage worth eur 3 billion in lost crops and eur 1 billion in damaged buildings. the commission proposal, which aims to close a major gap in current union legislation by reducing emissions of air pollutants from medium combustion plants, contributes to the achievement of the union's climate and greenhouse gas reduction objectives. i voted in favour of this report because air pollution is a serious threat to the environment and i believe it is essential to promote a credible climate policy at eu level based on compliance with air quality standards and emission limit values.
in writing. ‒ i am voting in favour of this report, which harmonises the rules on emissions.
in writing. ‒ today's vote fills a longstanding loophole in the legislation and regulates medium combustion plants by setting limit values for old and new plants. this is a good compromise which will make it possible to protect the health of european citizens better without at the same time excessively affecting the competitiveness of the industrial sector. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. the vote we have just taken on the report by the envi committee is very important: the amendments proposed to the commission proposal improve the chances of realistically implementing the directive on emissions from medium combustion plants, making it an important instrument for improving air quality in the european union without imposing unjustified burdens on society and the economy. it was an area where the regulatory vacuum was likely to cause uncertainty and damage to the environment, and i welcome this important acquisition.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the limitation of emissions of certain pollutants into the atmosphere from medium combustion plants, since they are very widespread and have a wide variety of uses, being found in electric generators, domestic heating systems and industrial heat or steam systems: however, they are a source of emissions of pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. i therefore consider parliament's commitment to protecting air quality and the environment and to combating climate change to be of paramount importance and therefore support a legislative proposal which for the first time regulates emissions from these plants. i also welcome the negotiating approach towards the council, which is to maintain the commission's regulatory proposals without any backtracking or weakening of the legislation: the air and environmental quality is a public good of fundamental importance to our citizens and as such must receive the utmost attention from the institutions. the regulatory approach, combining environmental protection with the proportionality of the charges imposed, distinguishing between old and new installations and focusing on smes, allows for an important decision which will benefit our society and also our companies.

in writing. ‒ there are around 150 000 medium combustion plants in the eu, i.e. combustion plants with a rated thermal input between 1 and 50 mw, used for a wide range of applications (electricity generation, domestic/residential heating and cooling, heat/steam production for industrial processes, etc.), which are a major source of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and dust emissions. by approving this proposal, we intend to make a significant contribution to the reduction of nox, so2 and dust pollution by setting limit values for existing and new installations and also by establishing a simple registration system, to make a significant contribution to the fulfilment of the member states' emission reduction obligations, while also avoiding possible trade-offs between air quality and the increased use of biomass, which in turn could lead to increased air pollution. the aim is to avoid duplicative regulation and excessive administrative burdens, while maintaining the objectives of the original legislative proposal. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'air quality' in the definition of the environmental criteria.

in writing. ‒ the report aims to reduce emissions of certain pollutants into the air from medium combustion plants. such systems are widely used in europe and are used in a number of fields: electricity generation, domestic heating, heat generation for industrial processes, etc. air pollution is estimated to cause over 400 000 premature deaths each year and to have quantifiable health costs of up to eur 940 billion, as well as a significant negative impact on the environment. in the eu, small combustion plants are regulated by directive 2009/125/ec and large combustion plants by directive 2010/75/ec, while medium combustion plants are not regulated at eu level. i therefore believe that the establishment of a system of regulation and registration of these plants at european level is an important tool for improving the quality of air emissions in the european union, for achieving the union's climate and energy objectives and for reducing greenhouse gases. i therefore decided to support this report by voting in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the new directive limiting emissions into the atmosphere of certain pollutants from medium combustion plants. these are some 143 000 installations used mainly for electricity generation, domestic heating and the supply of heat or steam for industrial processes. this fills the gap in european legislation on air quality in the combustion sector, which currently provides for two directives for small and large plants. noting that in many regions air pollution levels still remain above the limits set by the union and air quality standards do not even meet the objectives identified by the world health organisation, the directive introduces limits on emissions of pollutants created by the combustion of fuel in medium combustion plants not yet regulated at union level as they are increasingly contributing to air pollution, in particular due to a wider use of biomass, induced by climate and energy policy. this measure is therefore useful in reducing air pollution and consequently the serious risks to health and the environment arising from poor air quality.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report, which further weakens the european commission's already weak proposal to impose limit values on emissions from medium combustion plants. regulating and containing emissions from medium installations is of fundamental importance to protect the environment and human health and to reduce the social and economic costs of air pollution: we have therefore asked for two things in the committees. first, to tighten up the emission limits, to match them with what is possible to achieve through innovations in existing technologies. secondly, to include dioxins, furans and mercury among the pollutants subject to an emission ceiling. our efforts, unfortunately, have been in vain. not only that: the report put to the vote by the european parliament provides for even longer time limits for the entry into force of emission limits than those outlined by the european commission and increases the number of installations exempted from the application of the directive. we have tabled an amendment in the plenary to include at least offshore platforms among the installations subject to the directive: it was not approved. in light of all this, i had no choice but to say no to this relationship. and i said it with regret: we wasted an opportunity.

in writing. ‒ in early 2014, the commission published the proposal for a directive to harmonise the different laws of the member states on caseins and caseinates intended for human consumption. the final text proposes to amend some parameters in order to bring them into line with international standards. the document provides for a maximum moisture content of casein in foodstuffs of 12% (compared to the previously provided 10% parameter) and a maximum fat content of casein in milk in foodstuffs of 2% (compared to 2,25%), as well as the obligation to label the percentages on the finished product. it is therefore a package which i support, which ensures that european consumers have better controls and standards of food safety.

in writing. ‒ we voted today in favour of the adoption of this commission proposal to align the eu's financial regulation with the provisions of the new directives on public procurement and the award of concession contracts. in particular, with regard to crisis management measures under the common foreign and security policy and related civilian missions, the obligation to apply general union rules has often caused significant delays in the provision of essential equipment and services and had a significant negative impact on the functioning of the missions. the eu's credibility on the international stage is at stake at a time when the union is making important commitments to peace and security. we therefore believe that specific rules and more flexible procedures should be introduced, which move away from the current case-by-case approach and thus ensure rapid deployment in line with logistical and security requirements. such rules would also ensure adequate protection of the financial interests of the union in the context of the pursuit of the key eu security objectives, better meeting the imperative of sound, effective and efficient financial management as a result.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament's report on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the union, because i believe that the eu euratom regulation needs to be amended to ensure greater linearity in the procurement procedures of the european institutions. the amendment of several articles of the regulation adds precise selection criteria and access to european contracts to the procedure, automatically excluding from the tender administrations which have committed serious professional misconduct, fraud, corruption, participation in a criminal organisation, money laundering, failure to comply with obligations relating to the payment of contributions, taxes and fees, the financing of terrorism and child labour. in order to ensure a deterrent effect and to ensure that the attempt to obtain union funds improperly is not repeated, a financial penalty shall be provided for, as an alternative to or in addition to the exclusion from the tender, and, in the most serious cases, the publication of the information relating to the exclusion. particular attention is also paid to environmental protection and sustainable development by setting minimum standards to be met in accordance with international environmental law and national environmental protection standards. european funds will thus be more closely monitored in accordance with the principle of transparency and publicity.
in writing. ‒ i support all the amendments, especially those concerning transparency in the use of eu funds. i therefore decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ the european commission has presented to the european parliament and the council a proposal to align the financial regulation with the provisions of the new directives on public procurement and the award of concession contracts. the proposal includes an amendment to article 190 on 'external action contracts'. civilian missions under the common security and defence policy (csdp) are normally carried out in a crisis context and within a limited timeframe. their operational implementation is often delayed precisely because general eu procurement rules are not adapted to these situations. these delays contribute significantly to preventing the union from fully and effectively realising the potential of its external action. i therefore hope that specific rules can be adopted to ensure better protection of the union's financial interests in pursuit of the eu's key objectives in the field of security and foreign policy. i therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal on the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the union, which aims to revise the financial regulation following the adoption of the new directives on public procurement and the award of concession contracts.
in writing. ‒ the measures adopted today are aimed at improving fairness and transparency in the public procurement process and in the award of concession contracts by the eu institutions. i have shared the european parliament's view, because i believe that these new financial rules will effectively prevent tax fraud and misappropriation of public funds.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the reform of the financial rules applicable to the general budget of the union because the new text, revised in accordance with the procurement directive adopted in 2014, introduces significant improvements for the protection of the eu's financial interests, such as the possibility to negotiate contracts at interinstitutional level and the introduction of new criteria for compliance with environmental and social legislation. the reform text includes safeguard clauses to prevent organised crime from infiltrating the procurement procedures, by providing for exclusion criteria for fraud, corruption and participation in criminal activities, and by creating a database to detect illegal practices, developed in collaboration with olaf. this was a decisive point for my voting position. in addition, the measures adopted will improve reporting on the protection of the eu's financial interests and the performance of european funds, making data more accessible and transparent. finally, the reform optimises the time-limits for the transmission of the reports produced by the european court of auditors and streamlines the transmission of internal audit reports for discharge.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, the new procurement directive was adopted and it was therefore necessary to revise the corresponding articles of the financial regulation to bring them into line with eu legislation. articles 101 to 120 were revised with the key points relating to the possibility of negotiating contracts at interinstitutional level, with criteria for compliance with environmental, social and legislative standards and exclusion for fraud, corruption and participation in criminal activities. during this review, parliament also fought to open negotiations on certain articles of the financial regulation that needed to be revised after the 2012 approval. improving the reporting on the protection of the eu's financial interests and the performance of the european funds in the annual activity reports (articles 58, 60, 66); the reference to the transmission of documents useful for discharge (internal audit report) (article 99) and the rationalization of the timing of the court of auditors' special reports (article 163); optimisation of information procedures on landing and follow-up reports (article 166); the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the following: the procedures currently in place have therefore been optimized and i have therefore voted in favour.

in writing. the recent crisis that began in 2008 has necessitated a series of stricter regulations to protect citizens and savers. the crisis has also shown that the special structure of the european credit market is heavily imbalanced in favour of traditional banks, which provide the bulk of credit in circulation. when these enterprises were in a liquidity crisis on the one hand and subjected to stricter regulation on the other, it was the real economy, and in particular small and mediumsized enterprises and individuals, that suffered first and foremost. now that the recovery is beginning to show tangible signs, the commission has felt it necessary to support it by increasing the flow of liquidity into the system, which means first of all diversifying the types of credit, reducing the role of banks, but above all breaking down national boundaries, giving rise to a real single market for capital. we must welcome this decision, since it will really benefit the productive sector, young people and families. we are, however, waiting for assurances on some of the key points of this project, first of all the consequent increase in the risk of contagion.
the reporter . madam president, ladies and gentlemen, vice-president of the commission, tomorrow we will be adopting the compromise text on the new directive on payment services in the internal market. this directive is in addition to the regulation on interbank commissions drawn up by mr zalba and completes the package of legislative proposals on the european payments market presented by commissioner barnier during the last legislature, a package which i also shared and supported in my previous capacity as vice-president of the european commission. the final compromise was supported by all the political groups and was unanimously approved by the econ committee. i therefore thank the european parliament's negotiating team, which, under the leadership of president ferber, has achieved excellent results during the difficult negotiations with the council. i also thank all the shadow rapporteurs who have actively contributed to the drafting of a good legislative text. in europe, the retail payments market is dynamic and has undergone a lot of renewal over the past few years. 34% of europeans now shop almost exclusively online and over 50% own a smartphone, giving them access to the world of mobile payments. for some sectors of the economy, such as the travel sector, the majority of sales are now made exclusively via the internet. the measure we are about to adopt will regulate internet payment services, i.e. those services which intervene in the relationship between the merchant and the buyer's bank, allowing payments to be made without a credit card. the new rules will also cover the activities of the current account information services. these services provide the user with aggregated online information on one or more accounts used to make payments. it is a service which allows small businesses and craftsmen in particular to have a general overview of their financial situation at any time. the final agreement will also reduce the risk of fraud. all payment service providers will be required to adopt secure, authenticated or encrypted communication technologies, which will be regularly assessed and updated by the european banking authority. the main beneficiaries of the new directive will be consumers, who will benefit from reduced costs and greater legal protection. the amendments proposed by parliament and adopted will also bring a number of benefits to consumers: first, they will receive information on the transactions carried out free of charge; secondly, they will be entitled to unconditional reimbursement in the event of fraud and unauthorised payments. we are also solving the problems that citizens and businesses face every day when making payments online or via mobile devices. we are also opening up the market to new players and reducing the costs of an overly fragmented and expensive system, whose total cost today is about eur 130 billion a year. the new directive which parliament will adopt in its final form tomorrow will strengthen the competitiveness of the european payments market by encouraging innovation and security in a sector which is undergoing constant change. given the exponential growth of electronic commerce, the new rules will give a decisive impetus to the development of a single market that is increasingly geared to the needs of consumers and businesses.

author of the book. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner cañete, red mud is waste generated by industrial aluminium production and the red mud incident that occurred five years ago in hungary is the basis of the oral question in this debate, as it was an environmental disaster of european dimensions. on 4 october 2010, the rupture of a collection basin in hungary caused the leakage of approximately one million cubic metres of red mud with high alkaline content, which flooded several villages, killed ten people and injured about 150 others, as well as polluting large areas of land, including four sites in the natura 2000 network area. the accident highlighted the waste disposal problems of the mining industry, the shortcomings in inspections and also showed that these problems can lead to sometimes tragic consequences. there are also technical and economic difficulties that local authorities and civil society have had to face during the rehabilitation phase. i think a lot of things have to change if we really want to prevent such disasters from happening again in the future. of course, there will always be a risk, but our aim is to improve the level of efficiency of the mining industry and to significantly reduce the likelihood that events similar to what happened in hungary five years ago will occur again. as regards prevention, member states are called upon to review their permits for such industrial sites, in view of the correct classification of waste. the directive on waste management and extractive industries must therefore be fully implemented and we ask the commission to monitor its full implementation. member states also need to strengthen their environmental inspections and monitoring regimes, we already asked the european happened after 2008. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the prevention of the dumping of waste. we also need support similar disasters and to eliminate the pollution caused by mining.

member of the commission.– mr president, i want to thank all the participants in this debate for the very constructive declarations. first of all, i will refer to a question from mr gerbrandy, mr jávor and mr frunzulică, which is the question of implementation of directives. the commission is monitoring the implementation of the directive on the management of extractive waste – mainly on the basis of reported information submitted by member states referring almost exclusively to legal adaptation processes, but the commission services are exploring additional ways to obtain a more integrated and broader picture of the implementation of the directive on the ground. and, when needed, the commission has launched legal proceedings to address identified shortcomings in the transposition or implementation of this legislation. legal proceedings on extractive waste have been opened for hungary, for instance, as well as for denmark, italy, poland, portugal, romania and spain, inter alia. the commission is also in the process of identifying the main areas where further action may be required. as a first step, based on reporting from member states, the commission plans to submit a report on implementation of the directive to the european parliament and the council at the beginning of 2016. as a further step, the commission will carry out a more in-depth assessment of the level of implementation of relevant provisions of the directive. all this information will allow the commission to identify implementation gaps and best practices and take additional action to promote compliance with the objectives of the directive. as regards inspection issues, while acknowledging that enforcement and inspections remain key issues in the hands of the member states, the commission is currently considering the follow-up to be given in this respect and in the wider context of compliance assurance, as set out by the seventh environmental action programme. specifically in answer to ms kyllönen on the question of legislation on hazardous waste, the european waste list has recently been modified to ensure, inter alia, that red mud is assessed for hazardous properties. when classified by the member states as hazardous waste it would be subject to strict control requirements, provided for in the waste framework directive, for its management, labelling and transport.

commission communication to the european parliament and the council on the european strategy for energy security, cooperation with neighbouring countries within the energy community. at the end of 2014, the energy union was launched. the presidency considers that this was a major step forward, a qualitative leap in the development of european energy policy and in the strengthening of security of supply. this union has five equally important dimensions: security of supply, a fully integrated internal energy market, energy efficiency, emission reduction and, finally, research and innovation. on this last point, i would like to recall that the presidency recently organized the energy technology week in luxembourg, which brought together more than 500 experts in the sector, energy ministers and business leaders, including entrepreneurs in the field of renewable energies. the energy union also puts forward the strengthening of regional cooperation in the field of energy, which will allow for greater integration of markets while saving and creating energy in terms of investment. in addition, in the context of the implementation of the energy union and, more specifically, of the strengthening of the security of gas supply, the council expects the european commission to present, as i understand it, in 2016 a set of proposals on the supply of natural gas. the presidency shall follow the preparatory work, including at the level of public consultations on these issues. more specifically, the council has not yet adopted a formal position on the nord stream gas pipeline extension project. it is a commercial project between russian and western companies. the presidency is fully aware that this project involves energy, economic, geopolitical and environmental challenges. it raises questions, in particular as regards the project's contribution to the diversification of routes and energy sources in the union and its impact on other countries. the commission, as guardian of the treaties and of compliance with union law, is responsible for examining the draft in the light of the legal framework established and, in particular, the rules relating to the internal market. the presidency would like to assure you that this matter is being followed up in the council. it also continues to advance the implementation of the energy union and, in particular, the strengthening of the security of supply and energy independence of the european union, including the development and promotion of renewable energy. energy and climate today, we hear a lot of messages about climate are, in this respect, closely linked.
member of the commission.– mr president, honourable members allow me to start by reinforcing a key message: ensuring secure and resilient energy supplies to european citizens and companies is a top priority for the commission. in the coming months alone we will put forward a review of the gas security of supply regulation, publish a new comprehensive liquefied natural gas (lng) and gas storage strategy and propose changes to the intergovernmental agreements (idas) in order to make sure that they are in line with european security-of-supply objectives. that is also why we have committed to diversifying our energy sources, suppliers and routes. the goal is simple: putting an end to overdependence on a single supplier or route and giving member states potential sources of gas, be it pipeline gas from different sources or energy storage. in this regard, we will tap into a rapidly growing energy market which will allow us to more than double our imports from around 40 million m3 to up to 90 million m3 by 2020. we will invest in doubling our storage and accelerate the work on better interconnections between member states. we are making good progress in this area. in fact, in the last few months alone we managed to have the first tangible results in regions that are still insufficiently linked within the internal market. let me give you a few examples. the new high level group on gas connectivity in central, eastern and south-east europe will increase interconnectors in that region in the post-south-stream situation. the political agreement in july between spain, portugal and france on the development of the midcat pipeline will increase gas interconnection capacity within the iberian peninsula and the rest of europe. we are hopeful that midcat will be operational by 2020. work is also on track for our first delivery of 10 billion m3 per year of gas from azerbaijan to europe in 2020 through the trans-anatolian and the trans-adriatic pipelines. the restructured baltic energy market interconnection plan (bemip) will be our key instrument for integrating the baltic countries fully into europe. we will see that come to fruition this week when the agreement on the gas interconnector between poland and lithuania (gipl) will be signed. that project includes a planned contribution of almost eur 300 million. i cannot stress how important that work is, because, as it stands, the european union is still importing most of its gas from russia, about half of which currently crosses ukraine –and that brings me on to nord stream ii. the commission has taken note of the shareholder’s agreement to build further stretches of the nord stream pipeline. the first thing to say is that nord stream ii remains a commercial project and of course it will be for the commercial party to decide which infrastructure is valuable for them. but let me be clear, as with any other pipeline in the european union, this pipeline will have to comply fully with european union law, in particular the third energy package but also environmental, competition and public procurement rules. the commission will assess it rigorously against the european regulatory framework, and that assessment will be done on its own merits. transport capacity from russia is currently at a rate of around only 50%, and that already well exceeds the likely future needs of the european union in terms of supply. if constructed, according to our estimation, nord stream ii will further increase the excess transmission capacity from russia. i want to stress that the commission actively supports efforts to ensure that ukraine is and will remain a stable and reliable transit route. let finish by underlining the fact that the european union remains open for russian gas, and we would like to see russia as a reliable supplier of natural gas in the future, but we would also like to see that the transport of russian gas feeds into our diversification strategy and that the russian supplier, like any other supplier in the european union, plays to our competition and energy market rules.
the commission is concerned about the announced intention to double the capacity of nord stream. this would, as has just been mentioned, increase dependence on russian gas and reduce the transit routes from russia to the point of origin in the countries of the european union. today there are three: nord stream not doubled, yamal via belarus, the ukraine transit network, and it would become two. so there is a first problem of diversification of transit routes. reducing routes means calling into question the already weak balance between member states in terms of energy supplies. this is a major problem, especially for those who are currently engaged in the construction of the most ambitious project of european governance in energy policy, of which security of supply is a fundamental component. it is also a serious problem for the union as a whole, regardless of the exclusive dimension of energy policy, because cutting off ukraine from gas routes means weakening the consolidation process of this country and exposing eastern europe to heavy russian influence. the russian supplier announced that supplies to the ukrainian gts will end in 2020, thus foreshadowing for kiev the loss of many billions of euros paid to it annually in the form of transit fees; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the economic and social crisis. i would like to conclude by saying that south stream has been virtually sunk by this hypothesis and has been sunk by criticisms that today fit perfectly with nord stream.
