member of the commission.– mr president, i want to thank the honourable members again for their questions and comments on this very important issue of consumer protection and discrimination. this is an issue on which we can all agree that the current situation is not acceptable, when we look at the potential we are promising to our citizens and consumers in the internal market. in the current situation, we are supposed to have access to online and cross-border purchases, yet we cannot be fully guaranteed that because the offer is not available to another country, or because we cannot be sure of getting fair treatment compared to another consumer. the internal market is about offering everyone the chance to access – everywhere on eu territory – the services he or she needs, even from another eu country. i want to be clear: freedoms always have to be balanced against one another and there is not any which is more important than the other. so we need to balance contractual freedom with the right of consumers not to be unfairly discriminated against because of their place of residence. but we also need to recognise that there is no ‘obligation to sell’ or to unify prices throughout the single market. where this balance lies will depend on the outcome of the consultation and the discussions with the stakeholders and member states. article 20 of the services directive lays down the basic principles which member states should implement and apply. if a member state is in breach of these principles, the commission can initiate action against the member state. it appears that many member states have not taken sufficient action to put this principle of non-discrimination into practice. buying online has aggravated the current problems and a more comprehensive, effective and consumer-friendly solution is necessary. legislative proposals will be made by the commission as a follow-up to the digital single market strategy and the forthcoming internal market strategy.

in writing. ‒ since the introduction of the payment services directive (psd) in 2002, the sector has seen a rapid growth in the number of electronic transactions and the emergence of revolutionary mobile payment services, which have challenged the rules of this market. the aim of the psd ii reform, which was voted by the previous legislature in april 2014, was therefore to increase competition and efficiency in the payment services sector, while ensuring consumer protection first and foremost. the negotiations undertaken by the present parliament during the trilogues with the council, however, were far from satisfactory. although controls on access to personal information have been strengthened, while preventing fraud and abuse, the new text includes some derogations and exemptions. the directive does not cover payment services by debit cards and, in part, the telecommunications sector. in addition, important consumer guarantees already approved by parliament, for example on the right of withdrawal, are being removed and several derogations have been introduced for certain traders to escape the rules of the directive. the compromise reached during these negotiations once again underlines the subordination of the european parliament to the particular interests of the member states. for these reasons i have abstained from voting on this report.
in writing. ‒ the payment services directive (psd) of 2002 regulates payment services in the eu by setting out the rights and obligations of both payment service providers and consumers. the aim of its revision (psd ii) is to increase competition and efficiency in the payments sector, ensuring a level playing field for consumer protection. during the negotiations with the council, progress was made both in the inclusion of additional payment service providers in the directive and in the area of access to information to prevent fraud and abuse. on the other hand, the negotiating team had to accept a downward compromise on certain points such as an exemption for the telecommunications sector, the right of free withdrawal for consumers guaranteed only after 6 months and finally an increase in the threshold from eur 1 million to eur 3 million in annual transactions as a necessary clause to derogate from the provisions of the directive. these derogations make the text much less acceptable than the first version voted by the european parliament and i therefore do not think it is fully acceptable.

in writing. ‒ the death penalty is an instrument that violates the right to life, enshrined in the universal declaration of human rights, is ineffective as a deterrent and is irreparable in the event of miscarriages of justice. in addition, the poorest and most marginalized are the victims of capital punishment in most cases, as they lack the economic and cultural resources to cope with the costs and demanding procedures of a trial of this level. the death penalty also denies any possibility of rehabilitation and change of the person and affects the family members of the offender, who are not at fault for the actions committed by him. if we look at the data on its application over the last two decades, it is significant that the main promoters of capital punishment are non-democratic states, which apply it to intimidate minorities and target political or religious opponents, such as in saudi arabia, iran, china, syria, north korea and in many african dictatorships. the european union must therefore exert all its political weight to ensure that there is an international moratorium on the death penalty and its progressive abolition in all countries with which the eu has commercial or diplomatic relations.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the 'red mud disaster', an environmental incident which occurred in the town of ajka in hungary five years ago, caused by the rupture of a collection basin, with the release of approximately one million cubic metres of high-alkaline red mud, which flooded several villages, killing ten people, injuring nearly 150, polluting vast areas of land and wreaking havoc on the local flora and fauna. although the rapid and effective intervention of the national authorities and the activation of the eu civil protection mechanism by hungary effectively mitigated the damage caused to the territory, the incident highlighted the poor implementation of community rules. it is therefore necessary to strengthen national environmental inspection bodies, in particular by ensuring their independence and by providing them with adequate resources to enable transparent and cyclical inspections of industrial sites. i therefore decided to vote in favour of the text in order to give greater weight to the prevention of environmental disasters and to reach a legislative proposal on environmental inspections as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it asks the commission to provide a number of guarantees which i consider essential, such as: increased focus on research and development for the prevention and treatment of hazardous waste; strengthen national environmental inspection bodies to better carry out industrial site inspections; present a legislative proposal on environmental inspections and implement a financial guarantee system mandatory for all industrial sites and further develop the idea of an eu-wide mechanism for industrial disaster risk sharing, financed by a harmonised insurance premium at scale. the commission and the member states are also called upon to ensure the transparency of the financial aspects of the reparation of damage caused by environmental disasters, including financial compensation for victims. finally, i welcome the fact that our amendment on access to justice has been adopted.

points. first of all, there is a lot of work ahead of us in the 50 days we have before paris. we are not there yet. it is true that there are indices: at the moment, more than 150 countries have presented their indices. there is a high level of ambition but we are not within the two-degrees objective. under a business-as-usual scenario, according to the ipcc assessment, the increase in world instruments for long-lasting action towards fighting global warming throughout the century. we have to achieve full decarbonisation of our economies before the end of the century, and that requires a lot of effort. i want briefly to answer some remarks that members made: mr eickhout, mr groote, mr gerbrandy, mr liese and ms guteland asked what will happen with maritime and navigation transport. the commission considers that the international navigation and shipping sectors should also contribute to the global efforts for emissions reductions, because if we want a comprehensive and consistent agreement for below two degrees it must cover all sectors of the economy, including international transport. this should entail a mandate to the international civil aviation organisation (icao) and the international maritime organisation (imo) to deliver a concrete message on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from international aviation and shipping. those emissions should also be subject to regular review so that the measures can be enhanced over time, in line with decarbonisation scenarios. there was also a question to the commission concerning our position on earmarking eu emissions trading system (ets) allowances for international climate finance. ets auction revenues are one of the many public revenue sources that member states may use to mobilise climate finance, and the commission proposal for the ets revision actively encourages member states to use ets auction revenues to finance climate action. lastly, there was a question relating to fossil fuels. the commission is in favour of phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, and in the g20 framework we supported the united states proposal for a target date of 2025.

is going to do. i tried to explain this at the beginning but perhaps i should go into more detail now. i think we all understand the complexity of this matter. we europeans value the right to privacy from the side of the united states, that europeans’ data will be very well protected – and at least as well as we do it in the european union. this is our goal. you will understand that this is not easy to achieve because we are in the field of non-european jurisdiction. we also have to work with this fact. so what are we going to do? i am working intensively on a strategy to find a solution to situation. in the medium term we need to achieve good results in negotiations on the new, safer safe harbour and the new adequacy decision. i will come back to this. in the long term – and i also long term. this is what i wanted to stress at the beginning, asking you to help with your counterparts in the united states at your level. going back to safe harbour, safe harbour is a specific system which was created for transatlantic data flows. i am convinced that this system was created for a very good reason because the volume of the data transferred is extremely big and the data transfers are also extremely important for economic and commercial cooperation with the united states. this specific regime was declared invalid and now the conditions which are provided for by the data protection directive protection for international transfers must be applied. this is where we are now. but we understand – and i am convinced – that we need this new requested decision which will represent a new system which is something like a safer safe harbour. members are absolutely right that we need to look again at the 13 recommendations which were defined in 2013 as a reaction to the revelations about the extreme access of the security service to european data. we will look at those 13 recommendations in the light of the court ruling, which is the strong and clear benchmark for us in this retesting of these recommendations, because the court is in fact giving us new criteria for the assessment of adequacy. this is exactly what we are doing now. we start the negotiations tomorrow after a very thorough analysis of the court ruling. the negotiations will start tomorrow, and on friday on a technical level with our united states partners. we need to look again at all the all the criteria which the court ruling contained regarding the adequacy of data protection in the united states are feasible to achieve, but we must be much more assertive and much stronger now in in writing. ‒ the visa information system (vis) is the system for exchanging visa data for entry into the schengen area between the member states. the availability of exchange and comparison of such data by europol and the visa and border control authorities of the member states is important in preventing and combating terrorist activities and other serious criminal offences. in the fight against terrorism and criminal organisations, it is essential that the competent services have the most comprehensive and up-to-date information possible in their respective fields at their disposal in a timely manner. the availability of information and the speed of action make the difference between thwarting an attack or mourning its consequences. the creation of a single protocol regulating the handling of data and the possibility of access to it by police and investigative forces is important in reconciling the need for security and the fight against terrorist and criminal organisations with the right to privacy of every european citizen.
in writing. - i vote for it. the authorities will be able to cross-check in cases of serious crime or terrorism. the citizens need more security.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the draft resolution to set the date from which the decision on access to the visa information system (vis) for consultation takes effect. this structure should aim to improve the implementation of the common visa policy, also contributing to internal security and the fight against terrorism, according to well-defined and controlled parameters. in order to combat terrorism and other serious crimes effectively, it is essential that the relevant services have comprehensive and up-to-date information in their respective fields, so that they can properly carry out their duties. the data contained in the vis should therefore be available for consultation by national authorities and also by europol, which plays a key role in the cooperation between member states' authorities in the investigation of cross-border crime. this decision also has the merit of pursuing its objectives in full respect of the fundamental rights and principles enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, and that is why i have decided to vote in favour of the text.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the request for the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of béla kovács. on 3 july 2014, the president informed, pursuant to rule 9 (1), that he had received a letter from the hungarian prosecutor general requesting the waiver of the parliamentary immunity of béla kovács. the request for waiver of immunity shall be made in order to enable investigations to be carried out, on the basis of reasonable suspicion, to determine whether there may be a charge of the offence of espionage against the institutions of the union. any person who conducts intelligence activities to the detriment of the european parliament, the european commission or the council of the eu and hungary on behalf of a foreign power shall be punishable by a term of imprisonment of between two and eight years, as provided for in the hungarian penal code. according to information provided by the prosecutor general, kovács has had secret contacts with russian intelligence officials since 2010. the prosecutor has clarified that the investigation and possible subsequent prosecution for which the waiver of immunity is sought is limited to events occurring after 1 january 2014. moreover, there is no reason to suppose that a fumus persecutionis exists.
in writing. ‒ this is the proposal to lift the immunity of the member of the european parliament béla kovács, requested by the hungarian prosecutor general in order to be able to carry out investigations, on the basis of reasonable suspicions, to determine whether there may be an accusation against him in relation to the crime of espionage against the institutions of the european union under section 261/a of act c of 2012 on the hungarian criminal code. under that section, anyone who conducts intelligence activities to the detriment of the european parliament, the european commission or the council of the european union on behalf of a non-union country is punishable in accordance with section 261; the commission has also received comments from the hungarian authorities, which have not provided any information on the implementation of the measures taken by the hungarian authorities. for the reasons stated in the presentation above, i vote in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution entitled 'towards a new international climate agreement in paris', adopted in view of the 21st conference of the parties to the united nations framework convention on climate change (cop21), because i believe that at a crucial event it is crucial for the european parliament to reiterate the value of a final agreement in paris. the eu is very much involved in the negotiations and has already made its contribution last march. it has taken a clear stance on commitments to a 40% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in the eu by 2030. it is therefore a question of defending this position and committing ourselves to binding decisions. the european parliament believes that very important steps have been taken and that the objectives are moving in the right direction. however, they must be more ambitious, particularly in financial terms. i therefore hope that the paris agreement will be based on principles of equity and shared but differentiated responsibilities, based on respective capabilities and taking into account national circumstances, and will be a legally binding agreement and therefore able to provide a long-term response to the climate challenge for the coming decades.
in writing. we voted for the resolution containing the negotiating mandate for the european parliament delegation to the 21st meeting of the un convention of the parties, scheduled for early december in paris. the conference's goals include avoiding global warming of more than 2 degrees above pre-industrial temperatures. it is an ambitious goal, which involves a joint commitment by governments around the world to protect the environment and the climate. but our work only makes sense if we do it together with all the big players on the world stage and the main emitters of greenhouse gases, to defend our planet, without, however, penalizing our industries and their competitiveness. europe has always played a leading role in achieving these objectives and will once again play a leading role in enabling an ambitious agreement to be reached.
in writing. ‒ i support the report on the subject 'towards a new international climate agreement in paris'. a stable climate system is one of the greatest challenges in the fields of sustainable development and the world economy. the european union and its member states have committed themselves to the binding target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the eu by at least 40% by 2030. the aim of the report is to urge governments to implement concrete measures to combat climate change and to achieve a legally binding agreement in paris in 2015 to achieve this goal.
in writing. ‒ we are facing far-reaching and serious climate change. recognizing that this is one of the biggest challenges we face is the first step in moving in the right direction. as the honourable member points out, these objectives must aim at more ambitious and realistic results leading to greenhouse gas emission reductions of 50% by 2030 and increasing the share of renewable energy to 45% to achieve energy savings of 40%. in voting in favour of the report, i wanted to support the will to pursue an ambitious and effective policy which not only mobilises the instruments for climate and energy policy but also involves other key areas such as transport, research, innovation and trade or development cooperation. finally, a long-term response to the climate challenge must be provided, with the union and the member states working with institutions, ngos and other civil society actors to develop climate change mitigation initiatives.
in writing. ‒ climate change is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity in the fields of sustainable development and the world economy. they require an urgent, responsible and comprehensive response, based on the solidarity of the international community. in approving this report, we intend to support the commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. the eu and its member states have jointly committed to a binding reduction target of at least 40% by 2030. these objectives are moving in the right direction, but they should be more ambitious. the forthcoming paris conference will be just the beginning of a dynamic and evolving process that will allow the international community to take corrective action to realign itself on the trajectory needed to keep temperature rise below 2°c. we therefore expect a global and legally binding outcome, which will have to pursue a lasting and dynamic objective to guide and strengthen action against climate change, beyond the initial contributions submitted by member states. we need a forward-looking and effective policy for an energy transition by 2050, mobilising not only the instruments of climate and energy policy but also involving other areas such as transport, research, innovation, trade and development cooperation.
in writing. ‒ the socioeconomic metabolism of modern societies has produced numerous phenomena of environmental degradation. it was not until the late 1970's that the international community began to worry about the consequences of over-exploitation of resources. centuries of intensive and often uncontrolled exploitation, due to the inability of human society to combine environmental and developmental reasons, have produced many irreversible damages. the consequences are plain to see, and are particularly evident in the phenomenon of global warming, which is causing the global average temperatures of the air and the oceans to rise, snow and ice to melt widely and the resulting rise in sea levels. sustainable development is therefore the key challenge of the 21st century and requires that the principles of environmental sustainability be taken into account in all sectoral policies. this action must be carried out from the local level, with a constant effort to internationalize awareness of environmental problems in order to take the environmental issue to the global scale. the paris conference is an opportunity to take corrective action and to align ourselves with the european and un objectives of protecting the environment.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank everyone, and particularly rapporteur pilar del castillo vera, for their hard work on this file. we have come a long way since the commission proposed this legislation just over two years ago. it has been a bumpy road. i would like to thank this house, as it has only been possible to hold today’s landmark vote because of the european parliament. in april 2014, parliament showed that it can act decisively and quickly when the interests of the people, the open internet and the single market are at stake. today, i invite parliament to adopt this text on two key pillars in plenary so that consumers and businesses can benefit as soon as possible from common net neutrality rules and the abolition of roaming surcharges. they have been waiting a long time for this. adopting the telecommunications single market (tsm) regulation will be a major achievement for the digital single market. it will show europeans that the union can deliver tangible results. failure, of course, would have an opposite and demoralising effect. roaming surcharges will be significantly reduced from april next year and finally banned from 15 june 2017, subject to a fair use policy. this is a historic achievement, and we could not have done it without the leading role of parliament. many governments were initially reluctant until they heard the voice of their people and of the people’s representatives here. the package is faithful to parliament’s first reading position: there is a clear end—date for roaming surcharges and clear steps to be taken beforehand. there is still a lot to do for the abolition of surcharges to be sustainable throughout the european union. the wholesale roaming market has to be reviewed. the fair—use policies and sustainability mechanisms need to be defined. the commission has started to work on this. we are committed to making the abolition of roaming surcharges a reality. there is no justification for any further delay. adopting the tsm regulation will enshrine binding net neutrality rules into eu law for the first time ever. the regulation will create the individual and enforceable right for end users to access and distribute internet content and services of their choice. the net neutrality provisions also lay down rules on non-discriminatory traffic management and on end—users’ free choice of content, applications and services. these provisions cannot be circumvented through commercial agreements and practices. common rules on net neutrality mean that internet access providers cannot pick winners or losers on the internet or decide which content and services are available. they mean that the freedom of europeans to access or distribute internet content will not depend on the country where they are resident. this will increase consumer choice and competition, and will strengthen the digital single market. national authorities will be required to monitor market developments. they will have the powers and the obligation to assess traffic management and commercial practices and agreements, including pricing practices like zero rating. since this is a regulation, the rules are directly enforceable before national courts. the rules also give the necessary certainty for internet access providers and providers of content and applications to offer specialised services with quality requirements. adopting the tsm regulation will help to sustain continued network and service innovation. that will benefit both european businesses and consumers. let me turn now to radio spectrum. i welcomed parliament’s efforts to include the spectrum provisions in our original tsm proposal. these could not be retained because of the lack of council support at that stage. but the need to solve these issues remains, and i rely on parliament’s continuous support in the future. we have already started working on our telecoms review and look forward to close cooperation with this house. we plan to present an ambitious proposal by the middle of next year. i therefore welcome the call for priority to be given to a coordinated framework for spectrum in writing. ‒ we welcome the conclusion of the eu-switzerland agreement on the automatic exchange of information, which aims to improve cooperation and compliance with international tax obligations. it represents an important step forward in the ongoing efforts to combat tax fraud and evasion, improving on the 2004 agreement which guaranteed the application of measures equivalent to those of the eu directive on taxation of savings income. the automatic exchange of information on the financial accounts of their respective residents will therefore take place as from 2018. we believe it is essential that switzerland applies strengthened measures and respects the automatic exchange of financial account data promoted by the oecd global standards. it will cover not only income such as interest and dividends but also account balances and proceeds from the sale of financial assets. we share the rapporteur's view, however, that there is still room for improvement: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. finally, we call for the date of its entry into force, 1 january 2017, as agreed by the parties, to be respected without further undue delay.
in writing. ‒ believing that the conclusion of this agreement with switzerland is of particular strategic interest to the european union in order to combat tax fraud and evasion, which unfortunately exacerbate the already critical economic conditions in some member states, and in line with the rapporteur's request to ensure that it enters into force by 2017, i have decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ following the adoption of council directive 2003/48/ec on taxation of savings income, the eu signed an agreement with switzerland on 27 may 2015 on the automatic exchange of tax information. this agreement will allow the eu and switzerland to exchange automatically information on the financial accounts of their residents as of 2018. the exchange of information will include not only income from interest and dividends but also balances and proceeds from the sale of financial assets. the common objective is to be able to deal with situations where a taxpayer seeks to conceal capital consisting of income or assets that are subject to tax evasion. i believe that this agreement represents an important step forward in the fight against fraud.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of parliament's position on the agreement between the european union and switzerland on the fight against tax fraud and tax evasion. the agreement provides for the automatic exchange, as of 2018, between the tax administrations of the member states and switzerland of financial information relating to their respective residents, in order to limit the possibilities for taxpayers to avoid reporting to the tax authorities by moving assets or investing in products in switzerland. by effectively ending eu citizens' banking secrecy in switzerland, the agreement marks an important milestone in the eu's fight against tax fraud and evasion. as switzerland remains a crucial player in the financial sector, we must seek to ensure the utmost transparency in our relations through enhanced tax cooperation at international level.

in writing. the european parliament was consulted on the eu-switzerland agreement on taxation of savings income in the form of interest payments. the agreement should represent an important step forward in efforts to combat tax fraud and evasion. the aim is to deal with situations where a taxpayer seeks to conceal capital consisting of income or assets that are subject to tax evasion. the rapporteur, mr jeppe kofod, has made some proposals which we can all agree with. in particular, it requested that automatic exchange of information be introduced, that more transparency and frequency be introduced in the exchange of information and that the planned entry into force on 1 january 2017 be respected. although the proposals have added value, we believe that more was needed. we believe it is of the utmost importance that the exchange of information be automatic, compulsory and above all public. the agreement between the commission and switzerland is still weak in this respect. it is essential that agreements such as these are based on transparency. the progress made so far is not enough in our view. we also regret that parliament has only been consulted on such an important subject. for these reasons, we abstained from voting in the chamber.
in writing. ‒ through this agreement, the european union and switzerland commit themselves, as of 2018, to a constant and automatic exchange of information on the financial accounts of their residents. the aim is to combat, through close cooperation, the concealment of capital consisting of income or assets resulting from tax evasion. the tax authorities of switzerland and the member states will thus be able to establish clearly and precisely the identity of taxpayers and to determine whether acts of tax evasion or avoidance have been committed by natural and legal persons with the support of financial institutions established in third countries. the eu-switzerland agreement on the exchange of financial information undoubtedly plays a major role in the strategy to combat and counter tax fraud and evasion. that is why i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of repealing the directive on taxation of savings income. in 2003, the eu savings income taxation directive was adopted as a measure to ensure the payment of tax on savings income, and its provisions came into force in 2005. the revised directive was finally adopted in 2014 and should apply from 1 january 2016. in the meantime, the 2011 administrative cooperation directive was revised to align it with the oecd global standard for the automatic exchange of financial information for tax purposes and was adopted in 2014. it should also apply from 1 january 2016. the 2003 savings directive provides for the reporting of data on accrued interest on loans and similar products, while the administrative cooperation directive covers a much wider range of products. in the context of the fiscal transparency package of march 2015, the commission proposed to repeal the 2003 directive in order to avoid the application of both directives, thus avoiding the inconvenience caused by the dual data collection and reporting systems.

in writing. ‒ the proposal for the implementation of this council decision aims to authorise poland to receive and supply personal data pursuant to council decision 2008/615/jha as from the date of entry into force of the decision. under the latter, on the strengthening of crossborder cooperation, in particular in the fight against terrorism and crossborder crime, the provision of personal data in the context of that decision may not take place until the general provisions on data protection have been implemented in the national law of the territories of the member states concerned by the transfer. on the basis of an overall assessment report, the council concluded that the three abovementioned countries have fully implemented the general provisions on data protection set out in chapter 6 of decision 2008/615/jha. for these reasons, i have decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ i am voting in favour of this report for a better exchange of data and information.

in writing. ‒ i am in favour of the report on the exchange of dactyloscopic data in poland. the council has assessed that the state has fully implemented the general provisions on data protection set out in decision 2008/615/jha. the purpose of this decision is to strengthen crossborder police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters between the countries of the european union by providing that the provision of personal data may not take place unless the general provisions on data protection have been implemented in the national legislation of the territories of the member states concerned by the transfer.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the recommendation for the second reading on the council's position at first reading with a view to the adoption of the european parliament and council directive on package travel and package-related travel services. tourism plays a major role in the union's economies and travel, holidays and package holidays represent a significant share of the tourism market. however, the market has undergone profound changes in recent years, as the internet has added to the traditional distribution channels, changing the offer of tourist services, making them increasingly personalised. many of these combinations are not covered by the framework provided for in directive 90/314/eec and it is essential to update it. the new directive not only extends protection to all recent developments in the sector, but also considerably increases transparency and strengthens legal certainty for travellers and traders. i have therefore decided to approve this text.
in writing. ‒ the european commission launched an initiative in 2010 called 'europe, the world's number one tourist destination' to give tourism a new impetus. however, since may 2013, the commission has stopped drawing up the implementation plans and it is therefore difficult to assess the progress made now. i therefore voted in favour of this report, which calls for an implementation report to verify the actions undertaken, including the use of financial resources. one of the main problems with european legislation on tourism is that the resources allocated to it are really negligible and that most of the actions undertaken require funding in different funding programmes which are not integrated with each other.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the efdd group's proposal to reject the measure in question. as tourism services are the most popular category of products purchased online, the european legislator has stepped in to adapt the protection of travellers to the challenges posed by new technologies. to this end, the european commission has proposed a regulation amending directives 2006/2004/ec and 2011/83/eu and replacing directive 90/314/eec. the report makes it clear that this is a directive of complete harmonization in the interests of consumers and service providers. the new provisions apply to both the online and offline business travel sectors and substantially change the insolvency protection mechanism. in addition, travellers are offered the possibility to replace their package with an equivalent package in the event of a unilateral change by the organiser to a main element of the travel contract. the proposal lays down penalties and clarifies the scope of traveller protection for the purchase of combinations of travel services by including in the definition different forms of online packages and package tours. the derogations for ancillary contracts are extended to cover ancillary services provided as part of the package and the concept of 'travel assisted organisation', renamed 'linked travel organisation', is clarified.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this proposal because i think that in order to best protect the very important tourism sector in europe, it is very important to block those practices whereby tourist services, offering online packages, offer additional services in a hidden, obscure or ambiguous way. i am always against any kind of fraud in order to have a europe that is as serious, transparent and clean as possible, especially in a sector such as tourism where europe has a serious competitive advantage and cannot lose it because of a lack of confidence. it is a matter of protecting the businesses which, on a daily basis, are devising ways of offering services to tourists, but it is the greatest bulwark of defence for our lands, so rich in history and culture, but often impoverished by unfair commercial practices.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this regulation because i agree with the changes that are intended to be made in the field of package travel and tourism services. first, digital modernisation is essential in our era to make services more competitive. the amendment of the insolvency mechanism is of particular importance, as it provides greater protection for travellers. in addition, the clarification of the concept of 'assisted travel' to 'connected travel' also allows travellers to take an equivalent package when the organiser unilaterally changes a main element of the travel contract. this new legislative amendment will increase consumer protection and make tourist services more modern and competitive.
in writing. ‒ the extraordinary wealth of europe's artistic and landscape heritage makes the tourism industry an important element for growth in europe. however, this industry must remain competitive, including through greater protection of travellers. the european parliament resolution, which comes after a long legislative process, ensures greater harmonisation and transparency of the rules on package holidays and linked tourism services and greater protection for travellers, thereby strengthening the european tourism market. that is why i voted in favour of the resolution.
in writing. ‒ the approval of the agreement reached with the council on package travel and assisted tourism services updates and makes more effective the european legislation governing the sector of purchases of package travel, still unchanged from the 1990 directive 314, when the internet and online purchases were not widespread. i am pleased that the directive has strengthened the level of consumer protection by comparing the purchase of traditional travel packages and tourist services with those purchased online. in particular, the rules which have been approved today will allow 120 million travellers to buy personalised packages, enjoying the same rights and protections as those who buy pre-packaged or assisted tourism services. the change and evolution of consumer and business needs in the travel market, due to the advent of the digital age, necessitated new regulatory intervention by the european institutions. the adoption of the new directive will now ensure that consumers are better protected and informed about their rights.

in writing. ‒ in recent years, the role of travel agencies has been reduced as a result of the growth in the supply of low-cost flights and the sale of online travel packages. the previous 1990 directive on assisted package holidays is considered a successful and useful example of consumer protection for all-inclusive travel. since the way in which travellers plan and purchase their travel has changed substantially since then, a review of the legislation was necessary in order to broaden the definition of 'package holidays' to include self-booked online travel services. i therefore voted in favour of this reform which will certainly give consumers and travellers greater protection, including the possibility of withdrawing from the contract in exceptional and unavoidable circumstances, an opportunity which has not been provided for until now.
in writing. ‒ i have expressed my support for the report on package holidays and linked travel arrangements, which adapts a 1990 european directive on the protection of travellers to changes in the travel market, with particular reference to online booking of travel. the revision of the legislation we have approved will significantly strengthen the rights of travellers who buy tourist services online. in fact, those who buy a package on the internet with the formula 'all inclusive' or through linked web pages will receive the same protection as those who buy a package from travel agencies. in addition, travellers will be given more options to cancel a contract, through more information on their rights and who is responsible in the event of problems, such as the insolvency of the service provider. i particularly appreciate the rapporteur's approach, which has managed to combine consumer protection with the economic interests of the industry, such as tour operators, travel agencies and hotel establishments.

in writing. ‒ i welcome today's vote, which takes a further step towards updating the existing european rules on package holidays dating back to 1990. many products available today are not covered by the 1990 directive and in other cases remain in a legal grey area. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and to monitor the implementation of the new rules and regulations. among the safeguards which will ensure effective consumer protection, it is important to emphasize the availability of all the specific information before signing a contract and the possibility of cancelling a package in the event that, before departure, its price should increase by more than 8%. the new directive will also extend the definition of package holidays to include many services which can now be booked online but were not covered by the 1990 legislation.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report because it introduces important new features for those who pack their own personalised travel packages, offering greater guarantees to the user and defining the seller's responsibilities. the improvements include cancellation of the holiday without penalty if the cost of the package increases by 8%, a maximum of three additional nights free of charge if the return journey is delayed due to particularly adverse weather conditions, repatriation and full refund in the event of the seller's insolvency. the package travel directive was necessary because the existing legislation dates back to 1990, when the only packages in existence were those created by tour operators. today, thanks to the internet, the consumer can instead customize the package offered, choosing transport, hotels and other services, such as car rental, with the consequent difficulty of identifying the person responsible for the individual services within the package. the new directive thus covers package tours packaged by the tour operator, personalised packages assembled by the consumer and purchased by a single operator and assisted tourism, i.e. the combination of services sold by a single intermediary but as separate services, to which the principles laid down in the directive of 25 years ago are also extended.
in writing. the legislative proposal for a 'european single market for electronic communications' was sold to citizens as a big step forward, as the end of roaming charges and as the much-sought-after net neutrality. reality is not like that: first of all, there is no reason to postpone everything to 2017, except to take more time. roaming is changing, companies will be allowed to "spread" it to all users and if the stay abroad of the specially created "average user" is exceeded, it will become chargeable to the individual user. net neutrality is no more, there will be a lucky few (the bigs) who will enjoy high-speed bandwidth, while the rest will just have to resign themselves. this gives the operator the ability to "censor" any page by degrading it to its own unquestionable "like" to the slowest band. the amendments voted on were aimed above all at affirming net neutrality and eliminating ambiguous or explicitly negative exceptions. i voted in favour of these amendments, but unfortunately they were all rejected.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the new regulation on the european telecoms market, whereby parliament approves the end of roaming charges in the eu as of 15 june 2017, on the basis of a difficult agreement with the member states. the regulation also introduces a common framework on the right of access to the internet, in the spirit of sharing and free trade that has animated the global network ecosystem since its inception. this spirit, embodied in the principle of net neutrality, has enabled the web to evolve to become, according to tim berners-lee, "a central infrastructure of our time that permeates every sector, from the economy to the private lives of individuals". therefore, while sharing the important objectives achieved by the final text, i chose to underline further my position in favour of net neutrality by voting for an amendment calling for even more defined common rules so that the internet remains an open and horizontal platform, capable of promoting the right of everyone to access and distribute information, or to exercise free choice in the use of applications and services, avoiding fragmentation due to different national regulations. only by further strengthening the freedom and openness of the network can europe establish itself as a competitive, prosperous and just society.
in writing. ‒ this regulation says that all traffic on the internet should be treated equally but allows the opposite to be done, as it sets out a wide range of exceptions to the rule, allowing the possibility of managing data traffic and/or establishing preferential fast lanes. they will presumably be routed only by direct traffic to sites able to pay to make access faster and easier for users. i voted to reject the regulation as a whole, as it kills net neutrality in the eu. i voted in favour of the amendments which aimed to prevent all these exceptions. they failed. without net neutrality, google and facebook would not have been able to take their first, difficult steps towards popularity: the eu is effectively preventing the emergence of european innovative platforms that can compete with the us giants, as net neutrality is now being eroded. the abolition of roaming in the regulation is also limited to: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's telecommunications policy is not subject to the same conditions and is subordinated to the interests of telecommunications companies. that is the second reason why i voted no: the unconditional abolition of roaming would be a necessary step towards making europe a connected continent.

in writing. ‒ i welcome the interinstitutional agreement between parliament and the council which was expressed in the house today. i believe that this agreement will bring tangible benefits to our businesses and our consumers and i am pleased that a battle fought for a long time by my political group, the end of roaming, has finally been successful. we have today adopted a balanced regulation which breaks down artificial national boundaries and barriers, thus taking an important step towards the creation of a fully unified telecommunications market. i find the agreement particularly satisfactory because, in addition to the abovementioned end of roaming charges for european citizens, the new telecommunications regulation will also guarantee an open and non-discriminatory internet based on the principle of net neutrality.
in writing. the agreed text, which emerged from the negotiations between parliament and the council, appears unsatisfactory. on the one hand, the end of roaming is postponed to 2017, and on the other hand, the rules are designed to allow telephone operators to spread lost earnings on other tariffs, to the detriment of consumers. the privileged position which the telephone companies have acquired over the years is not being eroded and the courage to defend the interests of the community effectively is lacking. the commission is also prepared to throw out the possibility of establishing net neutrality in a clear and unambiguous way, which is essential if we want to create a truly free, competitive market, committed to innovation and transparency. the concept of net neutrality is replaced by an ambiguous definition of 'open access' which does not put all european citizens on an equal footing when accessing the services and content available on the net. this situation makes it possible to strengthen the dominant positions of large operators and service providers, while disadvantaging independent suppliers. i therefore voted in favour of the amendments, in order to restore a clear definition of net neutrality which is a real guarantee of freedom and equality for all citizens.

in writing. ‒ i considered that i would vote in favour of the amendment to directive 2011/16/eu, implemented by directive 2014/107/eu. the previous framework, which defined the legal framework for administrative cooperation on the exchange of information, required the exchange of a very small amount of information on tax rulings. directive 2014/107/eu builds on the principles of the parliament's resolution of 21 may 2013 in which it underlined the leading role that the eu should play in the fight against unfair tax practices. it introduces a new article, defining the scope and conditions for the mandatory automatic exchange of information on types of cross-border tax rulings and transfer pricing arrangements. this obligation is extended to judgments issued in the 10 years preceding the date on which the proposed directive takes effect and which are still valid on the date of entry into force of the directive. the proposed directive also provides for the possibility for the commission to set up a secure central repository where information communicated under the directive can be recorded.

in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of parliament's opinion on the proposal for a directive on the automatic sharing of tax information between member states, put forward by the commission in the wake of the lux leaks case to ensure greater coordination and coordination between member states in tax matters. in this text, we in parliament have criticised the agreement reached by the economic and financial affairs council on 6 october, which we consider to be a missed opportunity to achieve real tax justice for european citizens. the council's position restricts both the scope of the draft directive on automatic exchange, limiting it to crossborder tax schemes only, the commission's access to this information and the non-retroactivity of the directive on tax schemes already in operation. in the face of such an unambitious position, we believe that the proposals put forward by the commission and parliament should be taken seriously to ensure the greatest possible transparency for the benefit of citizens and national tax authorities.
in writing. i voted against this report in which parliament expressed its position on the revision of the directive on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation, which is necessary to respond more effectively to the challenges posed by the phenomenon of tax avoidance by multinationals, which exploded with the luxleaks scandal. while proposing some steps forward, this report fails to focus on the only really effective weapon available to combat aggressive tax avoidance, namely the full transparency of information on tax rulings, the tax agreements between multinationals and governments which have developed thanks to secrecy. we have fought for the creation of an easily accessible public register of all information and data relating to tax rulings, a simple implementation tool, strongly supported by civil society, but which has not found the consent of that part of parliament which is most sensitive to the interests of multinationals and powerful powers. that is why i voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ council directive 2011/16/eu was adopted to replace an earlier directive on mutual assistance between member states (council directive 77/799/eec) in order to respond to the need of member states to enhance administrative cooperation in the field of taxation. the purpose of the proposal was to strengthen effective and comprehensive administrative cooperation between tax administrations by establishing a mandatory automatic exchange of information on advance cross-border rulings and advance transfer pricing arrangements. the european parliament's main objective in this report was to remove any reference in this directive to the cross-border dimension of rulings, i.e. to extend their scope, while improving the timing of their notification, although i would have preferred a longer period of retrospective assessment. i would also have liked greater transparency, guaranteed by having a public register accessible to all, in which the data relating to the tax agreements signed would be entered. i therefore voted against, although i admit that some improvements have been made in comparison with the present situation.

in writing. i voted in favour of the decision not to grant discharge to the council: this is the seventh consecutive year that the european parliament has decided to send this politically strong signal in response to the council's decision not to recognise parliament's role in the discharge procedure. the council refuses to answer the questions which parliament sends to all the institutions and bodies of the european union on the statement of expenditure. in this way the council denies european citizens access to data on its administrative expenditure, effectively excluding the possibility of democratic control over the use of european citizens' money. the only body directly elected is parliament, and one of its tasks is to grant discharge after verifying that expenditure is correct. failure to recognise its role means diminishing all european citizens in their democratic role as voters.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because the council does not ensure the necessary transparency in providing financial information and reporting on expenditure, as the other institutions do. parliament asked the council for detailed information on the progress of the building projects and the management of the expenditure incurred so far, but received no reply. transparency is a key value in these cases.
in writing. ‒ for the seventh consecutive year, the european parliament has proposed, in the first instance, to postpone the discharge to the council. the report confirms that parliament is not in a position to take an informed decision on granting discharge and therefore calls for no discharge to be given to the council. the council's position is that the commission should be able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the budget is properly implemented. the report begins by pointing out that the council has not provided any explanation for the increasing level of under-utilized appropriations and commitments in its 2013 budget. in addition to raising the issue of administrative transparency, the council's attention is also drawn to the need to make the costs of the europa and residence palace buildings transparent. that is why i feel it is my duty to refuse to grant the council discharge.
in writing. ‒ looking at the recent ebola outbreaks in sierra leone, guinea and liberia, we applaud the international ngos, who immediately recognised the gravity of the situation and were at the forefront of fighting the virus as it spread. the rest of the world watched, probably hoping the fires would go out on their own. the delay in intervention caused thousands of deaths and, as we well remember, a risk of infection that went beyond africa's borders. at the moment, the interventions imposed by the imf and the world bank are only making an already tragic situation worse by actually requiring budget cuts in the public sector, for example in health care. the costs of dealing with humanitarian emergencies far outweigh the investment that can prevent them. the report calls for lessons to be learned from the ebola experience and denounces the unjustifiable international silence. that's why i voted yes.

in writing. ‒ although the media attention on the ebola crisis and the epidemic is waning, we cannot let our guard down in the face of a virus that continues to claim lives and from which we must learn many lessons. the management of the epidemic by local health services and international institutions has shown us how much work remains to be done to build effective health systems in the countries most affected by the disease, and how much needs to be done to address the structural shortcomings in prevention, hygiene standards, medical infrastructure and equipment, sufficient and properly trained health personnel, and access to medicines and basic health care. the eu has long been at the forefront of the drive for universal health coverage and the report we voted on continues in this direction, reiterating the will to allocate at least 20% of development aid to basic social services, including health as a priority. of course, it is also essential that the commission and the international community commit themselves to coordinating and strengthening in parallel efforts in the research and production of medicines and vaccines that are effective not only against ebola but also against other potentially lethal infectious diseases that are likely to develop into further epidemics.

in writing. ‒ in the wake of the volkswagen scandal, the european parliament debated a motion for a resolution tabled by several political groups, which was intended to be a political manifesto of commitment to halting emissions cheating by car companies as soon as possible. the text that came to this house was the result of tough negotiations between the political groups and contained some agreeable indications for everything that is expected to happen in the near future, from measurements of emissions on the road to vehicle type approval. that is why i voted in favour of its approval. but at the same time we wanted to make it possible for the citizens to know the names of those who continue to represent industrial interests in parliament. that is why we tabled amendments in the house which the main political groups had dropped from the original text and which provided, among other things, for the extension of the investigation to all brands and the obligation to return the tax incentives which had been granted to the car manufacturers whose fraud had been established. the names of those who did not want the return of public money allocated to the purchase of less polluting cars are thus available to anyone who wants to know.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on emission measurements in the automotive sector because i believe that parliament has an obligation to express its opinion on such a sensitive matter. i think it is important to stress the importance of the difference (not so much emphasized in the text) between the emission limits that pollutants can create and the respect of the rules already in place in europe. the case which gave rise to the decision to write a resolution arises from the failure to comply with european standards which are already concerned with the health of citizens and the environment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on emission measurements in the automotive sector, in which parliament takes a clear stand in favour of transparency and the protection of human health. with this resolution, we support the european commission's call for national authorities to carry out in-depth checks on various types of vehicles to detect any fraud in emissions tests and to sanction those responsible appropriately. we also call on the commission to adopt and implement as soon as possible a new system for testing emissions from real driving, extending the verification of emissions from nitrogen oxides (nox) to other pollutants. the resolution calls for the establishment of a european supervisory authority to conduct the tests in full independence and transparency. these measures are necessary to remedy a situation which threatens to jeopardise not only the entire european automotive industry but also the eu's air quality policy aimed at protecting the health of european citizens.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution but i think it is grossly lacking in transparency and accountability from the commission, which has done nothing despite knowing about the 'discrepancies' between the emissions of some vehicles during laboratory tests and actual emissions. the polluter pays, but the cheater pays too. we are facing a fraud against the states which for years have provided incentives to buy 'greener' cars at the expense of the taxpayer. we will fight for exemplary punishment, not just monetary punishment. we must denounce those who are covering up the activities of a faulty industry and in particular the fraudulent activities which have been carried out over the last few years by vw. the resolution we voted on was intended to be a strong criticism of what has happened and to underline the need to identify those responsible. in the course of the negotiations which led to the joint motion for a resolution, however, the name volkswagen disappeared from the text and only the forward-looking concepts survived, without any further commitment to identifying those responsible for what happened.
in writing. the future actions and the considerations set out in the text of the resolution are certainly to be welcomed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the fact that the community is not able to meet its own needs. i would also like to express my concern about the consequences along the supply chain, particularly for smes, which are facing enormous difficulties because of the fraud that has taken place. however, despite my vote in favour of the resolution, i would like to express my regret at the rejection of our proposals which called for equally important actions, such as the extension to all member states and to all car manufacturers of the obligation to carry out thorough checks on the emissions of vehicles produced, the refund in the event of irregularities of any tax incentives, if any, the need for detailed, accessible and transparent information on the checks carried out and the establishment of a committee of inquiry by the european parliament following what has happened. so despite the goodness of the text proposed, i think that some of the most important points could have been implemented more effectively.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the joint motion for a resolution on the measurement of emissions in the automotive sector because it is unacceptable that the european consumer is misled about the real value of polluting emissions from vehicles. emissions which, among other things, have harmful effects on health and the environment. the commission must take appropriate investigative action and must commit itself to a european authority to monitor the implementation of the legislation in force. finally, we must ensure that the effects of the wrong decisions of top managers do not fall on the workers.
in writing. ‒ i have personally pushed for parliament to adopt a resolution on emission measurements in the automotive sector. the credibility of our institutions and our industries at international level is at stake today. it is more appropriate than ever to call for fraud in emissions testing to be thoroughly investigated and to stress that those responsible must be sanctioned appropriately. i think the resolution is timely and measured, particularly where it calls for the eu's emissions testing system to be strengthened. i would remind you, in conclusion, that although those responsible for fraudulent behaviour will undoubtedly be sanctioned, this must in no way harm the workers in the industries involved, who must not pay for mistakes made at management level.
in writing. i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution because it represents a small step towards transparency in order to establish responsibility for failure to comply with environmental and consumer protection standards, and to punish offenders. the text, although with some limitations, calls for the establishment of an impartial european authority in the field of car tests, for an investigation into the case, including the fault of those who remained silent, for the recovery of european funds used and for the application of appropriate sanctions. i believe that more can be done to improve european governance of the automotive sector and to open infringement proceedings against manufacturers who have falsified their tests. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's internal market is not undermined by the introduction of new technologies. the european commission must also be held accountable for its inaction in the light of internal reports prepared by the research centres which show that the irregularities had been known for at least four years.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today the european commission, meeting here in strasbourg, wanted to send a strong signal about the adoption of the 2016 work programme, saying that it is no longer the time for conventional management. i would therefore like to highlight some cross-cutting and strategic issues which will certainly require 'unconventional measures'. whatever the practical configuration of the 2016 work programme, it is important to draw on some of the lessons that the european union has learnt in 2015. first of all , the greek lesson: the dynamics that have led one eu country to experience widespread and pervasive poverty must be prevented; we expect to see a major legislative implementation in this area. the lesson from libya and syria: the failure to act strategically has put us in dangerous and urgent situations. the european union has a long-standing commitment to the development of a european security and defence policy. the volkswagen lesson: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject. what if the fraud had involved food or pharmaceutical products? vice-president of the commission. – madam president, we are here today to discuss how to make best use of the eu budget to respond to the significant challenges the eu is facing. for the draft budget the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner andriukaitis, the subject of gmos is always the subject of heated public debate, particularly on the possible consequences for human health. to date, there is insufficient evidence to show that the consumption of gm foods can have any consequences for human health and the environment. efsa is expressing its position, but as you know very well in europe we apply the precautionary principle and so of course we have a very careful position on the subject. before i go into the substance of the proposal, however, let me thank my colleagues who have worked with me for what they have done so far. on 22 april, the european commission presented its proposal to amend the regulation on genetically modified food and feed, which provides for the possibility for member states to adopt national decisions aimed at restricting or prohibiting the use of gmos in food or feed, once such use has been authorised at union level, the so-called 'opt-out'. the envi commission has spoken out against the proposal, albeit with different reasons for its rejection. the majority was, however, large, with 47 votes in favour. during these months serious concerns were expressed regarding the lack of an impact assessment, the compatibility of the measures taken by the member states with the internal market and the feasibility of the proposal. the proposal was not preceded by an assessment of all the possible consequences and alternative options available. we therefore have no means of judging with certainty the consequences that the proposal may have for the functioning of the internal market in food and feed and for the competitiveness of the agricultural sector in the union. i believe that the proposal could seriously damage livestock production and also negatively affect agriculture in the european union, since the european union is still heavily dependent on the supply of proteins from genetically modified sources, and whereas the proposal is likely to have an indirect negative effect on imports. i also have serious doubts, which i have already expressed on several occasions in discussions with the commission, about the feasibility of the proposal, given the absence of border controls in the european union. the reintroduction of such internal controls, with barriers between member states, would be tantamount to erasing the economic achievements of the european customs union and the single market. and we cannot think of having a leopard-spotted internal market, after all the efforts that have enabled us over the years to eliminate internal barriers, the internal borders of the eu. it is also not clear how member states benefiting from the opt-out can ensure the practical enforcement of the measures on their territory. so we are here today in the plenary to take a decision in this parliament and the rapporteur's request to his colleagues is to reject the proposal. we shall also be voting on a number of amendments to the legislative resolution: the commission has already made a number of proposals, some calling for a new proposal from the commission and others calling for a moratorium until a new proposal is made. as rapporteur, i would also like to ask you to vote against these amendments, because i believe that the legislation in force is good legislation, but the member states must have the courage to apply it. the member states must of course take their responsibility. we are therefore sending a strong signal to the commission with today's vote and i hope that during the debate our colleagues will be able to give a full account of the reasons for our opposition.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too join in the appeals made by mr boylan and mr staes. commissioner andriukaitis, president juncker last year committed himself to making the process of authorising gmos more democratic. this proposal is not standing, the impact assessment is missing. there has therefore been a lack of political will to make a serious effort to resolve this situation. parliament is expressing itself in its text. we have tried to propose amendments to suggest ways of resolving this situation, to encourage debate. we, as the five star movement, believe that risk management could eventually be returned to the member states, so that they can be free to manage the health risk that may result from the release of these genetically modified organisms into the environment. or we could accept the greens' proposal to amend the comitology rules through regulation (eu) no 182/2011. so there are possibilities and solutions that can be put forward, which we strongly urge the commission to listen to in order to finally arrive at a proposal that is as democratic as possible and which allows member states and those who want to obtain and market gmos to have gmos on their market, and those who do not want them to finally have legal certainty.

member of the commission.– mr president, of course i have followed very closely this controversial debate and i have taken due note of all the comments and views that the honourable members, have expressed. i would like to reply to some of these. regarding the claims that the commission proposal is not in line with the european union single market rules, i will simply respond that this is incorrect. according to the european union treaties, member states may derogate from the freedom-of-movement rule on the basis of overriding reasons related to the public interest. that is enshrined in the treaties. this is not against the single market: it is about the right of member states to see such overriding reasons. we must follow the rule of law; we must follow the treaties; we cannot act without a legal basis – and the proposal fully respects that principle. i am in favour of supporting the single european market. i am in favour of supporting science-based assessment, because that is the only way. i believe in science – independent science. as regards the accusation that an impact assessment was not carried out, i would say this: it is meaningless for the commission to carry out an ex-ante impact assessment on a proposal which merely gives the member states a legal basis on which to act. in relation to cultivation proposals, the same logic applies. the proposal does not have an impact in itself: it will be up to member states to evaluate the possible impact of their own decisions – about which you have raised many, many questions. it is in the hands of member states to use the opt-out mechanism if they are ready to do so. they must follow the impact assessment procedure because this is a very serious and complex matter. i fear from the unwilling tone of the discussions that there is a real possibility of parliament rejecting the proposal. allow me to repeat my view: it would be preferable to continue to discuss this frankly and openly under the ordinary legislative procedure rather than to seek to close down the dialogue. i would repeat once again jean-claude juncker’s promise: the commission should be in a position to give the majority view of democratically—elected governments at least the same weight as scientific advice. it is about the member state governments’ view, not about the scope for treaty changes to change the voting mechanism, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the current novel food regulation is cumbersome and makes the approval and marketing of novel food products too slow: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. the agri-food sector, on the other hand, is a constantly evolving sector, which needs an up-to-date regulatory framework to keep pace with technological developments over the last 20 years, for example with regard to nanotechnology. the text we are about to vote on today is an important step forward in this direction, which should encourage innovation in the food industry through a genuine data protection system and at the same time lead to a reduction in the administrative burden and to simplification of procedures. however, in simplifying the current authorisation procedures for novel foods, a high level of protection of human health and consumer interests should also be ensured through a systematic centralised risk assessment by efta and a strict application of the precautionary principle. therefore, additional specific labelling requirements are needed to protect consumers.

commission's statements transitional national measures the commission takes note of the decision of the european parliament and the council to allow member states to keep existing derogations related to red coral harvesting without any time limit, and to provide for new derogations to be granted during a transitional period again without clear cut-off date. the commission considers that, by their nature, derogations and/or transitional measures can only be temporary and that the unlimited exceptional regimes agreed between the co-legislators may put the union in a position where it is not able to ensure that its international obligations towards the gfcm are fully respected. in the event that the above mentioned risks should materialize, the commission will submit proposals for appropriate measures in accordance with the relevant provisions of the treaty. in any event, the commission emphasises that any decision in this case will not prejudice the commission position in relation to other rules on derogations and/or transitional regimes. final date for use of rovs (remotely operated underwater vehicles) with regards to the final date of 31/12/2015, agreed by the european parliament and the council for authorised use of rovs for observation and prospection of red coral, the commission takes note of the decision of the co-legislators to interpret the words "until 2015" in paragraph 3a) of recommendation gfcm/35/2011/2, as "until 31 december 2015", thus deviating substantially from the commission's proposal to consider only the time period before 2015, until 31 december 2014. having already stressed that, by their nature, derogations can only be temporary, the commission recalls that also the fao legal service had expressed the view that only the time limit before 2015 should be considered. in the light of this, the commission will assess if appropriate initiatives need to be taken in order to clarify the union's position on the issue of rovs within the gfcm.
