the following is the text of the joint statement by the european union and the united states of america, the european union and the united states of america, on the situation in burundi (2015/2973 ((rsp)).
i now ask minister schmit to speak on behalf of the vice-president of the commission and high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. you change your cap...
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as has been said, the current head of government, since 2005, in refusing to comply with article 96 of the constitution, which prohibits the eligibility for a third term, has caused and is causing a number of problems in a country already in great difficulty. the risk is that the situation will deteriorate for reasons which my colleagues have already mentioned. in addition, burundi's population is 85% hutu and 15% tutsi, an imbalance that creates a number of problems between the two ethnic groups and raises concern in an area where the memory of the genocide in neighbouring rwanda is still alive. the tragedy could happen again and the threats are real and concrete. the president of the burundi senate has even spoken of the pulverization of rebellious neighbourhoods and the minister of public security has reminded the tutsi of their minority status, clearly stating that the hutu population could easily be incited to act against the tutsi. in this climate, freedoms and human rights are being increasingly restricted and human rights issues are being seriously questioned. the decision to close down ngos that receive foreign funding is the final straw. we can 't just stand by and watch this happen . europe has an important job to do. the european union has recently allocated financial resources to burundi under the european development fund 2014-2020, inter alia, to assist burundi in strengthening governance and civil society: the irony of fate! if the situation does not change, i believe that the european union must look at how to get out of this situation and use its financial resources to exert all the necessary pressure so that the political situation in burundi returns to normal.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, rwanda in 1994 was a tragic event. burundi 2015: the number of deaths another genocide? this question haunts my soul and the souls of many, as i think of the savage repression and the terrible violence that is bleeding the streets of this country. so far, the report says 240 dead and 280,000 displaced. the bodies of opposition figures and even their relatives, such as the son and son-in-law of pierre claver mbonimpa, a well-known human rights activist, are lying in the streets. the government continues to raise tensions: prevents ngos from existing; one minister even appeals to the nine million hutus to solve the problem if the police are not enough to stop the mainly tutsi opposition; a senate president incites genocide by quoting rwanda slogans. if we had been more decisive earlier, we might have prevented nkurunziza's third candidacy in violation of the constitution, which has started a fire that could affect the entire region. it is time to think about energetic sanctions against the current government, of all kinds, to suspend cooperation and to isolate those who are inciting hatred and violence, and to be ready for an intervention mission to defend civilians and the most vulnerable. if we do not do this, we may once again be blaming thousands of lives that could have been saved.

the statement by the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy on the elections in myanmar/burma (2015/2974 ((rsp)) is now on the agenda.
president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice—president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, on 8 november, myanmar held historic elections contested by 91 political parties and over 6 000 candidates. the people have voted for change, expressing a strong desire to live in a new, free and democratic myanmar. they have given a clear mandate to aung san suu kyi’s national league for democracy, with a solid majority in both houses of parliament, to take myanmar’s democratic and economic reforms to the next level. we are pleased to say that the european union has been at the forefront of international support for democratic transition in myanmar, and we very much appreciate that the european parliament has played a very important role in this respect. on 16 november, the high representative called aung san suu kyi personally to congratulate her on her election victory. she highlighted the crucial role that our 150-person-strong election observation mission, led by ep vice-president alexander graf lambsdorff, had played in the holding of peaceful and competitive elections. i would like to take this opportunity to thank graf lambsdorff for his commitment and his excellent work as eu chief observer. myanmar’s democratisation process is, however, not yet completed. the disenfranchisement of the rohingya and other ethnic minorities remains a matter of concern. in this election, unlike previous elections, the rohingya could not cast their vote or stand as candidates. none of the big parties fielded muslim candidates, apparently bowing to the strong influence of radical buddhist monks. in some ethnic areas no election took place, on security grounds. the eu eom preliminary statement points out that further constitutional, legal and procedural improvements remain necessary if totally fair and fully inclusive elections are to be held in the future. aung san suu kyi, the leader of the largest party in myanmar’s new parliament, is barred by the constitution from running for president. the military will continue to occupy 25% of parliamentary seats, and, regardless of who forms the next government, three key ministers will come from the army. in that context, all political actors will need to engage in dialogue and work towards a peaceful transition in a spirit of national unity and reconciliation. despite these challenges, we believe that we have witnessed landmark elections, offering a great opportunity to strengthen democracy in myanmar. the next critical stage will be the election of the new president in mid-february 2016 and the formation of the next government by the end of march 2016. although aung san suu kyi has yet to reveal the priorities of the new government, we can expect that democracy, human rights, the rule of law and economic development will be high on the agenda. while myanmar can count on our support, there are still issues of concern on which we will continue to constructively engage with myanmar. these include the discrimination against, and the statelessness of, the rohingya minority. the eu is also worried about buddhist radicalisation, which has resulted in legislation on the protection of race and religion that is not consistent with the country’s international human rights obligations. eu-myanmar relations have come a long way since 2011. with the exception of the arms embargo, sanctions were suspended in 2012 and then lifted in 2013. everything but arms trade preferences was also reinstated that year. an eu-myanmar task force, with the active participation of the european parliament, was set up in november 2013. the eu and myanmar have stepped up cooperation in the area of human rights. two rounds of human rights dialogue, led by the eu special representative for human rights, have taken place since 2014. myanmar ranks high on our democracy support agenda, and we will look into appropriate follow-up with a view to implementation of the recommendations of the eom, which will be presented early next year. in recognition of our assistance in the peace process, the eu was invited to sign the nationwide ceasefire agreement as an international witness on 15 october 2015. with other donors we are setting up a joint peace fund to further encourage the process. last but not least, the eu and myanmar are currently negotiating an investment protection agreement, and the eu is also part of a labour rights initiative, together with other partners. the eu defined its strategy and priorities in support of myanmar’s transition process in the comprehensive framework adopted by the foreign affairs council on 22 july 2013 and confirmed in the council conclusions. the main priorities for engagement, democracy, peace, trade and development and myanmar’s re-engagement with the international community continue to be valid. our bilateral development cooperation programme under the 2014—2020 multiannual indicative programme for myanmar amounts to eur 688 million and features four focal sectors: rural development, education, rule of law and peace-building support. this is fully in line with the country’s transformative agenda. the eu is also a key provider of humanitarian assistance for vulnerable populations, in particular stateless persons and displaced populations. as myanmar steps into the future, the scope of our engagement underlines the eu’s strong commitment to further supporting the country’s democratisation. the eu stands ready to play its part in helping to bring myanmar’s transition process to a successful conclusion.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i had the honour of participating in the parliament's election observation mission to burma/myanmar, led by my very good colleague mrs gomes. in burma, democracy has been won - or rather, destroyed - by aung san suu kyi's party, despite a constitution that still allocates 25% of seats to the military and three strategic ministries: the department of defense, the department of the interior, and the department of the interior's office of ethnic affairs. the atmosphere of this victory was felt by all of us in the voting: the european parliament has been the driving force behind the development of the community's relations with the countries of central and eastern europe. but be careful: although the situation has now started on a track that is difficult to reverse, we are still in the middle of a transition and we must be cautious until the official proclamation of the results. this is not only because it will be a long journey - i hope not decades - towards a government full of civilians and towards changing the constitution, but also because the change has been initiated thanks first of all to the heroism of suu kyi, many of her party and many democrats who have suffered unprecedented suffering. but it was also an impulse from the top of the regime itself, which does not want to give up all power. now he 's starting a new journey: the european union must also support burma, including in the face of the emergence of ethnic war. i visited the refugee camps on the thai border and saw thousands of people without identity, rights and future, suspended like their huts built in mud. the european parliament cannot stand idly by. burma must become a federal state that gives a home to everyone. the burmese people expect a lot from us and we must not disappoint them.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this election in myanmar tells us of a fundamental turning point in the history of the country: we finally have democracy back. i would also like to thank the colleagues who have had the honour and the duty to represent the european parliament at such a historic moment. but now the myanmar government faces some very difficult challenges: on the one hand, we must finally be able to completely reduce the influence of the military, which unfortunately still holds 25% of the seats. on the other hand, there is a country to rebuild, a country that today spends only 1.8 percent of gdp on health and only 0.8 percent on education. gdp growth must lead to an increase in the well-being and development of the entire population, and this goes beyond the fight against corruption but also goes beyond decisive action against discrimination against the rohingya population, one of the most persecuted minorities in the world. aung san suu kyi is fond of saying that fear is the only prison. we hope that there is no prison for change in myanmar and that we as the european union can only support this change.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, it is very important that we today affirm in concrete terms that children and young people have the right to education and to education, even when they are refugees or in emergency situations. sometimes we forget. there are 10 million refugee children, many of them in refugee camps in lebanon, jordan and turkey; others have arrived in europe. many of them have already lost years of schooling to the conflict. however, we know, as you have also stressed, that access to education and psychological support is not a second stage of reception but an integral part of it. it is also a powerful tool to save them from violence, trafficking, radicalization. it's a very powerful psychological aid, but it's also a planning element for the future for them and their families. despite the commitment of unicef, of many ngos, also of private individuals, of hundreds of teachers, also among the refugees themselves, the resources allocated so far we know are not enough and we very much appreciate that the commission has collected the proposal to double the share of humanitarian aid already since 2016. and we are also reiterating another proposal which we made in the culture committee, which was accepted, and i thank mrs mcavan very much, namely to create a humanitarian corridor, opening the doors of european universities to refugee students, including through distance learning.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, education is a very important instrument in the development of countries in crisis and prolonged emergencies. in these circumstances, we know that children are the most vulnerable, often victims of abuse and exploitation, including sexual abuse, or easy prey for recruitment by criminal organizations and armed groups. prolonged crises, however, can have devastating effects on the proper psychophysical development of children, with the risk of giving rise to the phenomenon of the so-called lost generation. in such situations, education is an effective tool for prevention and protection for children, with long-term positive effects on building resilience. and this is especially true for those children who have been separated from their families as a result of conflict or natural disasters. i thank the commission for its sensitivity, but i ask that it act promptly to draw up a comprehensive aid strategy, including education for children in emergency situations.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the education sector in emergencies and crises is currently among the most underfunded: it receives less than 2% of global humanitarian aid, enough to fund just one third of current needs. education must be considered a priority in these contexts, as it ensures a guarantee of protection for children, precisely at the time when they are most vulnerable. as linda mcavan used to say: school gives them a sense of normalcy. postponing educational activities until after the emergency has passed may mean that they never return to school, often condemning them to a future of poverty. and education is the best antidote to radicalization. let's make education support central to projects funded by eu trust funds and find platforms that break down the barriers between humanitarian and development aspects, that ensure continuity and coherence to these policies. it is time for the eu to become the first international donor to reach the 4% spending target in this field. i thank commissioner stylianides for his commitment and for the good news that we will be able to do so as early as next year: it is a good signal in the implementation of the sustainable development goals (sdgs) that we just approved in new york.
member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank members very much for this very important discussion. i have noted your perspectives and suggestions, including the last one about informal education and the one about distance learning. we have already discussed some initiatives through unrwa for palestinian refugee children. i would like to thank parliament very much again for this very special discussion. i am truly glad that we have such exemplary cooperation in this very difficult field. i would like to say a few more words on two issues. one is informal education, which is a practical solution in exceptional circumstances in countries whose formal capacities are overstretched. lebanon is an example of this. i visited the region again a few days ago and saw the practical value of such alternative mechanisms on the ground, in particular in the bekaa valley. informal education is also the necessary first stage for the integration into formal education of a child, or even an adult, who has been out of school for a very long time. this has, for example, been the case for children who were actively involved in conflicts in africa and the middle east. secondly, on linking emergency assistance with the eu’s long—term assistance, linking relief, rehabilitation and development, the so-called lrrd: this is very important, and i strongly welcome the fact that you referred to this extensively in the resolution. education ultimately requires a long—term perspective which humanitarian aid alone cannot provide. this is why, together with my colleagues commissioner mimica and commissioner hahn, we are working to ensure the complementarity of our instruments, as i have already mentioned, through new trust funds in africa and the middle east, to help in the syrian crisis. this is something which is already ongoing with many instruments, and there are several instances where eu children of peace programmes have been continued or scaled up by development instruments. i would like to say something about the engagement of the private sector in this respect. members know that a lot of money, for example in some gulf countries, has unfortunately not been utilised until now for the very specific purpose of education in emergencies. it is very important to see new global instruments, such as the new global fund, which may manage to utilise this money through private means. it is very important to allow this way to make a difference and to find solutions on the ground. it is not a dispute between the public sector and the private sector but something more than this. i would once again like to thank members for their strong leadership, especially my dear colleagues from the committee on development – linda and other colleagues. let us continue our efforts together. i would like to say that the real practical impact of these initiatives for education in emergencies is very important in showing the real benefits on the ground in conflict areas, such as the bekaa valley and the zaatari refugee camp, and inside syria. my next initiative is to find solutions for education in emergencies in the region around aleppo. thank you so much again for your collaboration. in writing. ‒ on 17 july 2014, negotiations with ecuador for its accession to the trade agreement between the european union and colombia and peru, signed in june 2012, were concluded. i voted in favour of parliament's motion for a resolution because this accession represents an important step forward in the alliance with the rapidly developing countries in the latin american region. ecuador has in recent years been committed to reducing poverty, from 37.5% to 22.5%, and has focused on improving social and environmental conditions. by joining the trade agreement, the country will be able to enjoy the benefits of trade with the eu, thus fostering further economic and social development. the union will also strengthen its economic relations with the latin american market, which is considered to be one of the fastest growing and most interesting markets in the world.
in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the agreement to include ecuador in the trade agreement between the european union, colombia and peru, which will allow an increase in exports to europe to the benefit of the ecuadorian economy. as a socialist group, we believe that trade is a means of achieving progress both in terms of the economy and the well-being of citizens, by opening up new markets but also by ensuring that investment serves to reduce inequalities and improve living conditions. this is what we hope for ecuador, which we want to include in the close links already existing with other south american countries, asking its government to establish a clear and transparent path on human, environmental and social rights as a condition for concluding the agreement, as was done with peru and colombia at the time of concluding the trade agreement in question.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the measure because the union institutions have made considerable progress towards simplification by adopting several measures, including the simplification programme of the multiannual financial framework 2014-2020. despite the focus on simplification methods in the reformed cohesion policy for the 2014-2020 programming period, the submission of applications, management, reporting and control in the framework of the esi funds remain complex for both beneficiaries and managing authorities. parliament considered that the commission should introduce detailed simplification guidelines to make member states and regions aware of their role in significantly reducing administrative burdens and over-regulation at national and local level in the context of procurement procedures, the selection of proposed projects and monitoring and control activities, for example by avoiding frequent changes in regulations, simplifying language and standardising procedures, and by targeting the eu budget towards achieving tangible results. it also called on the commission to engage in a structured and permanent dialogue with parliament, the committee of the regions and other stakeholders on all aspects of the simplification process.
in writing. ‒ despite the considerable progress made by the european institutions towards simplifying the rules and administrative procedures in the context of cohesion policy, there are still many bureaucratic obstacles to the proper functioning of the allocation of european structural and investment funds. in particular, it highlights the difficulties faced by both the beneficiaries and the managing authorities of the funds with regard to the procedures for submitting applications, managing, reporting and monitoring investments. the complexity of the procedures and the existing over-regulation are the main causes of this criticism. administrative simplification should be balanced with the detection and prevention of irregularities and fraud through the rationalisation and structured organisation of control, monitoring and reporting activities. in this regard, member states should commit themselves to significantly reducing the administrative and bureaucratic burden on citizens and small and medium-sized enterprises at national and local level and to monitoring procurement and project award procedures. i support the motion for a resolution as it seeks to simplify the rules of cohesion policy, making financial instruments more accessible to beneficiaries and improving their use.
in writing. ‒ this is a particularly sensitive and complex issue, which will be at the heart of both the 2014-2020 and the post-2020 implementation. the council and the commission recognise that good governance and administrative capacity are among the main prerequisites for achieving the objectives of cohesion policy and that the responsibility for improving administrative capacity lies with the member states and their regions, although supported by the commission. however, a dangerous prospect is to be avoided, whereby small and rich countries with limited financial allocations converge on a concept of simplification strongly linked to proportionality, which is translated into: financial dimension of resources, quality of governance, management of programmes, level of risk of regularity of investments. so the danger to be avoided is a two-dimensional world: all simple and light for the small and good group, and vice versa, multiple controls for those with many resources and weak management skills. simplification means paying more attention to the content and less to the pieces of paper and, above all, ensuring equal treatment between member states and interpreting the principle of proportionality correctly.

in writing. ‒ cohesion policy is the union's main investment policy, providing the framework and investment strategy needed for investments of the agreed growth objectives. the european union aims to achieve five concrete objectives by 2020 in the fields of innovation, employment, education, social inclusion and climate/energy. despite the significant progress made by the union institutions towards simplification, detailed simplification guidelines are still needed to enable member states and regions to eliminate or drastically reduce the over-regulation of procedures at national and local level.
in writing. ‒ the resolution proposal deals with the simplification of cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020. given the existing over-regulation, including the transposition of rules into national law, and the complexity of the procedures, which can place a heavy burden on small and mediumsized enterprises, ngos and municipalities that need eu funding, i feel i must support the position of my colleagues who have drawn up the proposal. it calls on the commission to introduce simplification guidelines to encourage member states to reduce the burden on national and local authorities in the context of various administrative procedures, such as procurement procedures, the selection of proposed projects and monitoring and control activities.
in writing. ‒ while recognising the progress made by the european institutions towards simplifying the esi funds system, the procedural rules on the submission of applications, management, control and reporting still define a particularly complex system for both managing authorities and beneficiaries. over-regulation, partly caused by the redundancy of legislation created by the transposition of community legislation, leads to a prolongation of time which, in turn, increases indirect costs for beneficiaries and reduces the impact of investments. the complexity of procedures and administrative delays are a deterrent for small and medium-sized enterprises, small local authorities and smaller ngos. in view of the facts, i can only welcome a resolution which promotes a simplification process which takes particular account of small and mediumsized enterprises and smaller local bodies. i am particularly in favour of the call on the commission to draw up simplification guidelines for the national administrative authorities responsible for managing the esi funds. i also support the reduction of the financial burden on beneficiaries and the establishment of a single desk.
in writing. ‒ i have always tried to support, through my parliamentary work, the need to make european funds more accessible to potential beneficiaries, in particular by simplifying the procedures for participation and making the parameters and evaluation mechanisms for submitted projects more transparent. the administrative burden and over-regulation, in my view, are an obstacle to the effective and efficient use of european funds by the beneficiaries, particularly by small and mediumsized enterprises. the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal to simplify the procedure for the adoption of the directive on the protection of the environment by the member states. i would therefore have voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ despite the progress made by the eu institutions towards simplifying cohesion policy, the application, management, reporting and control of esi funds remain complex, both for beneficiaries and for managing authorities, especially for those with fewer administrative and financial resources. this entails significant indirect costs for potential beneficiaries of eu funding. i therefore believe that simplification of existing legislation, language and procedures is necessary in order to achieve tangible results. that is why i am voting in favour today.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the measure on the simplification of cohesion policy for the period 2014-2020 as i believe that the procedures for accessing the european structural and investment funds need to be further simplified. member states should endeavour to significantly reduce administrative burdens and over-regulation at national and local level in the context of procurement procedures, the selection of proposed projects and monitoring and control activities.

first vice-president of the commission.– madam president, this morning in the commission we adopted an important package on the circular economy. it is the result of very intensive teamwork and it really is a pleasure to present this package to you today, together with vice-president katainen and commissioner vella. this is a really innovative way of working in the commission. we have worked together with more than half of the commissioners for a year to bring everything together because here, if we want to make this transformation, we need all areas of our activities. and so this novel way of working is something that is also the way forward: the way the commission should be working in the future. in the week that cop21 in paris has started, this is, i think, a very timely proposal. action on the circular economy ties in closely with our energy and climate policies. more and more evidence shows the wider benefits of the circular economy, including in lowering carbon dioxide emissions. there are many good reasons for moving away from our linear economic model, which is extremely resource-intensive. in a world where the population rises every day, with huge demands placed on land, water, food, feed, raw materials and energy, we cannot rely further on a ‘take, make, use and throw away’ approach. the circular economy, as an agenda for change, is not only an environmental necessity, it is the only model that makes sense in the long term for our european economy. it makes economic sense to use natural resources in a smarter way. europe cannot compete on wage costs, although sometimes we try – and we lose. and europe is not graced with the same natural resources as other parts of the world: they are finite in europe, and when they are available, they are very expensive. the future is in providing products that are used and reused and do not deplete the earth’s natural resources. it will also allow us to continue as a market leader for green technologies. so the question is not whether we want to set europe on a circular path of growth. it is rather how we, at our level, help our businesses, citizens and member states to get where they want to be, where they need to be, and to get there more quickly and in better shape. with the package we are proposing today, we want to give a concrete push to the circular economy and accelerate the transition. what we are presenting is an ambitious and comprehensive eu framework that europe needs to take action and make real progress towards the circular economy. it is an all-encompassing approach of smart regulation, market- based instruments, innovation and incentives. it is a clear signal to economic operators that we are simplifying the eu single market in this area to create new business opportunities and to boost the market for secondary raw materials. we want to be more ambitious than in the past by going beyond waste, with measures covering the full life-cycle of products, from the design of a product and production processes – and of better-informed consumption choices – to modern waste management. we want to back this up with our financial instruments and funds. our action plan and revised waste proposals adopted today are mutually supportive measures that will contribute to making real progress on the ground. while jyrki will shortly go into more detail on the wide range of actions we propose, let me say a word about our waste management proposals. continuously advancing on waste management remains a priority. with targets, and through incentives and support for recycling and reuse, we want to ensure that resources stay within the circle and are available for future use. waste is not managed as well as it could be. from the total waste production in the eu, only a limited share, 36%, was effectively recycled. the largest share, 37%, was simply sent for disposal, whether in landfills or on the land. losing this material means that significant growth and competitiveness potential is not being exploited. to fundamentally improve waste management practices we need eu waste legislation. the legislative package we have adopted today will provide a very clear and stable policy framework allowing public and private actors across the eu to develop long-term investment strategies focusing on prevention, reuse and recycling, and avoiding overcapacity in incineration. is it ambitious? well, let me say that this is most likely the world’s most ambitious legislation and probably contains the strictest recycling and land-filling targets on earth. our proposal will also reduce the administrative burden for smes and public administrations by improving definitions and simplifying reporting requirements. while reflecting a high level of ambition, our proposals also take due account of the different realities and recycling performance levels across the eu. differences today are huge, but our objective is to achieve gradual convergence to best-practice levels. efforts to close today’s implementation gaps will be supported by the eu cohesion policy, with eur 5.5 billion already available in the run-up to 2020. food waste is a particular priority area where we want rapid change. it is economically, socially and, quite simply, morally unacceptable that so much edible food is wasted every year in europe. in september we adopted the un sustainability development goals, including a target to halve food waste by 2030 at the retail and consumer level, and to reduce food losses along production and supply chains. the eu and its member states are committed to delivering on this target. with that aim, we will develop a reliable method to quantify and understand food waste in order to act on it efficiently. we will also work hand-in-hand with member states and stakeholders on a dedicated platform to support the achievement of our goal. if i may, i would now like to give the floor to vice-president katainen.
vice-president of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, it is a very big honour to be here to discuss with you the very significant package the commission has proposed. this is part of the european investment package. the circular economy is a phenomenon in the global market economy which one can compare to globalisation, which we have witnessed over the last two decades. so it is not just a side-effect or a secondary element of the market economy; instead it is a global mega-trend and will be even more so in the years to come. the package which we have proposed is more ambitious than the previous legislative package on waste. now we are completing the circle. now we can really talk about the circular economy package. this package is a competitive package and it is also a single market package. how ambitious it is can be measured partially also by the speed with which the co-legislators are dealing with the proposals that the commissioner is bringing forward. this is about empowering consumers and encouraging businesses to move from an inefficient and unsustainable linear economy to a circular market economy. the package is the beginning of the story. it will not transform the european economy from the current linear model in one go, overnight, to a circular economy. but at least, at the moment, with this package we can create a good start and a good basis and a good structure to further develop circular economy initiatives. the action plan will complement the two initial legislative proposals concerning waste. in the action plan there are proposals ranging from product design to creating an internal market to secondary raw materials, and further support for the industrial symbiosis by recognising the value of by-products. a key objective here is to work on further deepening the eu single market, which is also the most important part of the investment plan for the eu. this matters because there are barriers that make it difficult for businesses to optimise the resources used. that is why creating a market for secondary raw materials and ensuring a reliable quality standard is crucial. it is fundamentally about broadening our internal market. the ecodesign framework is a tool to strengthen development where products are easier to repair, dismantle and recycle. we will broaden the scope of ecodesign from energy efficiency to resource efficiency. ecodesign is an important tool, which will empower consumers and create a level playing field for businesses. we are also announcing a specific strategy on plastics – an important and complex issue. today only 25% of plastic waste is recycled, whereas half goes to landfills, with economic and environmental consequences. large quantities of those plastics end up in the oceans, creating marine litter. we will develop work to address all these issues based on the latest evidence. in addition to this, there will also be a revised regulation on fertilisers in order to recognise organic and waste-based fertilisers and to support bio-nutrition. also, there will be a legislative proposal on minimum standards for reused water for irrigation. public authorities, starting with the commission, will be encouraged to step up their uptake of circular economic criteria in public procurement. this has great potential for the circular economy, as public procurement makes up nearly 20% of eu gdp. we will therefore emphasise circular economy aspects in new or revised criteria for creating public procurement, and the commission will lead by example. finally, the commission strongly supports innovation to make the circular economy happen. we need to rethink our ways of producing and consuming. we need to create new technologies and business models, which will shape our future. in the horizon 2020 work programmes for 2016 and 2017, we are putting eur 650 million on the table for innovative demonstration projects. added to this, there are eur 5.5 billion in structural funds for circular economy purposes. in addition to this, efsi can finance projects which are either joint ventures between the private and public sectors or private investors. so by quickly implementing the proposals now, we can achieve both economic and environmental – but also societal – gains by transforming our linear economy to a circular market economy. let us give consumers an opportunity to lead the transformation by their choices, and let us strengthen competitiveness and create incentives to businesses to change their business models.

in writing. measures to achieve the quantitative targets for the presence of women at the top of the company must be taken. the paradox - which i would consider ridiculous if not dramatic - is that it is not wished to admit that the subject of women, whatever the context in which it is addressed, is a moral obligation which cannot be postponed and is based on a difficult change of mentality. this delay in the application of the 'principle of nature', of gender equality, results in a reduction of europe's economic potential, whereas growth in innovation, research, training and skills acquisition is never accompanied by the active participation of women because it is limited by the lack of inclusion of women in decision-making bodies. it is not surprising, then, that studies show that a greater presence of women in the labour force would increase gdp by 21% in italy, 19% in spain, 9% in france and germany and 8% in the united kingdom. in the correlation between the percentage of women on boards and the financial performance of companies, the net return on equity is 41% higher than that in which women are absent. these data do not require further comment.
in writing. the text of the proposal for a directive on the gender balance in the boards of directors of listed european companies, as it stands, is a perfect example of respect for the principle of subsidiarity. it is a law that proposes a more transparent and fair selection process, without providing for measures such as gender quotas, which have also proved to be in the countries where they have been introduced, including italy the most effective and fastest way to really combat discrimination against women in decision-making places. i understand that the last year and a half has been full of important events that have catalyzed the attention of all the european institutions, but we can no longer afford to consider gender equality a b-priority. we have already abandoned the proposal for a directive on maternity leave, again because of disagreements between member states: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we have an excellent compromise text today, the time for discussion is over and it is time to produce concrete results.
in writing. i hope that the council will soon reach agreement on this directive, the implementation of which would finally ensure a balanced representation of women on the boards of european listed companies. at a time when european women are still struggling to integrate fully into the economic and social life of the community, the adoption of this measure would symbolically and effectively confirm the equal vocation of the european union. the european parliament took up this challenge two years ago by voting by a large majority on the proposal. i therefore expect that the member states which have been reluctant to do so will also finally give up their reservations and accept the need for this. i am proud to point out one fact: the country i represent in the european community assembly, italy, has been a pioneer in this field, by passing a bipartisan law guaranteeing the presence of at least one fifth of women in the boards of publicly listed companies. i hope that the other european states will follow our example, overcoming their own perplexities in the name of the will to ensure the construction of a fully inclusive union.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report. in this report, parliament welcomes the special report of the european ombudsman on the own-initiative inquiry into frontex, supports the ombudsman's recommendation that frontex should deal with individual complaints of fundamental rights violations committed in the course of its operations; considers that the establishment of an individual complaint mechanism could offer individuals an opportunity to exercise their right to an effective remedy in the event of a breach of their fundamental rights and supports the need for an official central structure within frontex for the handling of individual complaints. the ep also recommends that frontex and the european ombudsman establish close cooperation with each other in order to improve the protection of individuals from similar acts of maladministration, and calls on the member states and partner countries to cooperate effectively with the agency to ensure the smooth functioning of the complaints mechanism. finally, it calls on frontex to provide publicly accessible information on the complaint mechanism in its annual general report.

in writing. ‒ i support the report on the establishment of an individual complaint mechanism in the event of violations of fundamental rights. this will enable individuals to exercise, either individually or through a third party, their right to an effective remedy, particularly in the case of violations committed against vulnerable persons, pregnant women or children. in addition, as recommended by the european parliament, frontex will have to ensure easy access for all to information on complaint procedures and to actively cooperate with the european ombudsman and each member state in order to ensure the smooth functioning of the mechanism and the protection of individuals in the event of maladministration.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the ep resolution on the european ombudsman's special report on the own-initiative inquiry into frontex, because i believe it is right and proper that migrants are treated in a humane and dignified manner and can have a mechanism to protect and report violations of fundamental rights. the increasing flow of migrants and the increased presence of the eu border agency frontex raise serious concerns about the respect of human rights. i therefore believe that the european parliament must make its voice heard in the face of the scenes we have seen and continue to see in some member states. i therefore welcome the initiative taken by the european ombudsman and the idea that the same agency should be able to deal with individual complaints of violation of rights, whether they are made by frontex staff or by staff seconded from member states. finally, i share the european parliament's call for the establishment of an internal complaint mechanism within frontex, which can be activated by the victim in the event of a violation of rights, involves the frontex fundamental rights officer and is transparent, accessible, translated into languages understood by migrants and guarantees the protection of the complainant.
in writing. ‒ frontex has faced many challenges in the past year. the worsening of the migration crisis has weighed heavily on the agency and has often called into question its various aspects, from its role to its financial allocation. i voted in favour of this report, which perhaps deals with the most important aspect. the greater the tasks and challenges facing the agency, the greater its responsibility. frontex operates in extremely sensitive contexts, where situations of danger and emergency clash with the fragility of the people being rescued and at the same time the need to carry out effective checks. the ombudsman has asked us to make frontex a fully-fledged agency, to make it accountable for the actions of its agents, and to create a mechanism to guarantee transparency and, above all, the right to complain to anyone who sees that his rights are not being respected. i believe that this is the direction in which frontex should grow, but ensuring that this does not hinder or slow down the other activities of the agency.
in writing. ‒ we welcome this report which supports the european ombudsman's recommendation that frontex deal with complaints about violations of fundamental rights in the course of its operations, provide adequate administrative support for this purpose and establish an independent complaint mechanism. the report was made necessary by the growing phenomenon of migration flows. the appeal mechanism requested is therefore very important in the light of the increased capacity of frontex, in particular as regards participation in the management of migrants in so-called 'hotspot' areas. it is also required that the appeal mechanism be supported by human rights actors. in addition, it is stressed that there should be a system where appeals are first checked and filtered to assess their admissibility, that the criteria for admissibility are clearly defined, and that appeal forms are translated into languages that citizens who make appeals can understand. finally, it is of crucial importance that those officials who have acted in violation of fundamental rights are excluded from any frontex activities.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by thanking the rapporteurs - mr eriksson, mr gróbarczyk and mr tošenovský - and all the members involved in these two draft reports. the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the energy union's objectives and to monitor the implementation of the energy union's objectives and targets. the commission fully agrees with these three elements, as already illustrated by the report on the state of the energy union adopted by the college a month ago and presented to this house by vice-president šefčovič, who has been encouraging and coordinating our action on this important priority for the european union. i would like to focus my speech on these three issues. first, the need to maintain the ambition levels of the energy union. i have just returned from paris, where for the past two weeks the european union, with its allies, has led the negotiations to reach the most ambitious climate agreement in history. but the execution of that agreement starts today. that means we have to meet our target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 40% from 1990 levels; we have to achieve a renewable energy share of 27% and improve energy efficiency by 27% by 2030 with a view to 30%. as far as renewable energy is concerned, we already have a 15% share in the european union, but we need to step up our efforts to make the 2030 target a reality. and so we will have to tackle the review of the renewable energy directive scheduled for the second half of 2016. as regards energy efficiency, let me reiterate that the commission is already looking at how we could raise the target to 30%, as this draft report calls for. the energy efficiency directive is also the worst implemented. we will therefore have to ensure that it is complied with in all the member states. but we also need to raise our ambition level. that is why, next year, i will be presenting a set of proposals related to energy efficiency in sectors such as heating and cooling, buildings and transport and industrial emissions. furthermore, i believe that a transition to a low-carbon economy must be driven by innovation and the european strategic energy technology plan will be key. the second issue i want to talk about today is the need to measure our progress, which is linked to the eriksson report on the 10% electricity interconnection target by 2020. today, only 20 member states meet these targets and for some, such as the iberian peninsula, the baltic states or cyprus, electricity interconnection is clearly insufficient. and, moreover, the lack of interconnection is an impediment to ensuring the integration of renewable energies into our energy matrix and to achieving greater shares of competitiveness. we will start 2015 with the inauguration of a new electricity interconnection across the pyrenees, and today we have inaugurated the new electricity interconnections between lithuania and poland, and between lithuania and sweden. both 'litpollink' and 'nordbalt' will be key to ending the energy isolation of the baltic states. and we have just adopted a second list of projects of common interest containing the most important interconnection priorities for the european union: 108 electricity projects that will enable 26 member states to reach the 10% interconnection target by 2020. but, returning to the draft report we are discussing today, i am particularly pleased with the ambition it shows in including the longer-term target of 15% by 2030. i announce that i will propose the creation of an expert group on energy infrastructure to monitor progress towards the 10% target and make proposals if the target is not reached, as well as advise the commission on how to reach the 15% target. one of the central pillars of next year's legislative proposals will be the design of the electricity market to achieve greater market integration. strengthening the role of acer and promoting closer regional cooperation, as the draft report indicates, will be key features of the market design proposals, and that will be of key importance for energy security. as the draft gróbarczyk report points out, we have made important progress in diversifying gas supply sources and routes. the next package on security of supply, which includes a review of the regulation on security of gas supply and a proposal to revise the decision on intergovernmental agreements, will help us to go further. and that's important because many countries are overly dependent on russian gas imports. and on that issue, let me respond to the concerns about nord stream 2 raised in the draft report. first of all, it is clear that this project, like any other, will have to comply fully with european union law. secondly, i would stress that the commission will only support projects which are in line with the objectives of the energy union, including energy security. and in this context, diversification of supply sources, routes and suppliers is key. finally, i would like to make it clear that the european union still considers ukraine to be a safe and necessary transit country. i will make sure that parliament is informed of any developments. and it is in this spirit that i come to my final point: the need for accountability. the state of the energy union made it clear that the energy union can only work if it is based on a reliable and transparent process anchored in legislation. over the next few years, we will be proposing a series of legislative proposals on the five dimensions. and here parliament, as a co-legislator, will have a decisive role. of course, alongside this we need a robust governance process, as underlined in the draft report on the energy union. as many of you have pointed out, this process would be meaningless if it became a mere bureaucratic process. that is why next year we will propose an initiative on simplifying planning and reporting so that, after 2020, member states develop an integrated national energy and climate plan; that the monitoring system is based on a report on progress made by member states; and that the commission assesses collective progress in an annual comprehensive state of the european union. in this context, the powers of this parliament will be fully respected. i would like to conclude by saying that the commission welcomes these two draft reports very much. we will ensure that the energy union remains an ambitious, responsible and measurable project. don't expect hard work. the next year will be decisive because of the large number of concrete initiatives included in the legislative programme for 2016. i will work with this parliament to make the energy union a reality.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are finally here. this parliament has its say on the energy union, the most ambitious strategy for the integration of europe's energy markets since that first bold and in some ways visionary draft: the european coal and steel community. well, more than 60 years later, the context and the world have changed a lot, but the theme remains the same: the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the energy policy and the energy efficiency of the member states, in particular by ensuring that the energy security of the member states is a factor of stability, competitiveness and growth in their territories, with an additional challenge, the crucial challenge of climate change and sustainable development. so it is in this spirit that we are voting, after weeks and months of negotiations, on the basis of a solid text to which almost all the groups have contributed and which puts this house back at the centre of the debate on the future of the energy union. these are the two points which i think are most important: the second point is the call for strong governance, with full ownership of parliament within the ordinary legislative procedure and for the indispensable objectives which we socialists and democrats, together with others, want to be even more ambitious in terms of efficiency so that the energy transition is bold and socially sustainable. so parliament is back on the field, ready to make its voice heard in the busy process of building the energy union, with the commitment shown in recent months by the commission in bringing the energy union through step by step and the obstinacy of this house in seeking broad consensus on the basic objectives, as conditions for important achievements, towards a single, harmonious and fair european energy area. all this is finally there, it is up to us of course to continue the work.

answer to a blue-card question. i believe that electrical interconnections between countries, even with the latest technologies, should be encouraged. as far as hydroelectric power is concerned, we are now, in many parts of europe, saturated with what is sustainable in terms of the protection of the natural environment. we must remember that hydroelectric power can still have problems as a result of climate change, which in any case puts the supply of hydroelectric basins at risk. however, we must also take account of this variable, which will become more and more serious in the years to come.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is absolutely necessary to create a sustainable energy environment, not only to ensure energy security, naturally by trying to reduce prices, but above all to achieve the climate objectives, such as, for example, respecting the global average temperature increase of less than two degrees, agreed at the paris summit. energy security also means diversifying supply, thus reducing dependence on fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, and focusing on renewable energy. we must work to make the energy union a real engine of growth and investment, especially in green energy, jobs and competitiveness, investing, as i said before, also in renewable technologies, clean transport, smart homes and new production methods; the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the application of this regulation. so to actually achieve a green economy, an economy that is in all respects sustainable, with positive repercussions not only on energy savings, and therefore from an economic point of view, but also on the reduction of the greenhouse effect. it will therefore also be necessary to review the energy label, because we must give consumers a clear and precise idea of what the information and savings for the citizens will actually be.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is coming out of the historic agreement reached at the paris conference on climate change strengthened. in addition to laying the foundations for saving the planet, it is a strength of the european union as a whole and a sure path towards a robust and stable european energy union, which is therefore the real institutional and political challenge. it is well known that the current existence of economic, regulatory and administrative barriers to energy consumption does not protect but rather exacerbates energy poverty. i therefore agree with the report and emphasize the key role of the issues of emissions trading, the necessary introduction of real driving emissions testing, the decarbonisation of the air, sea and land transport sector which is still excluded from binding commitments, the reintroduction of waste into the economy as a raw material for a true circular economy and the achievement of the 10% electricity interconnection target and the improvement of the functioning of the internal electricity market in the european union. all of these are key to achieving a secure, independent, inclusive, transparent and competitive energy union.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs cecilia wikström, for her work and all the other shadow rapporteurs. trade marks are of the utmost importance for the european production system and this is even more true for certain national subsystems, such as the italian one in which 'made in' is synonymous with indication of origin, quality, guarantee of the marked products and services. the reform of the eu trade mark regime is now reaching its final stage, not without difficulties and not without criticism. among these, we note the failure to introduce an explicit 'fair use' clause which would have allowed a broader interpretation of the limitations of the exclusive right, whenever it is necessary to reconcile the latter with the freedom of artistic expression. however, we found it desirable to include a special recital to guarantee respect for fundamental rights and freedoms, in particular freedom of expression. the guarantee introduced for the free movement of generic medicines is also very welcome, without neglecting the need to combat the trafficking of counterfeit medicines and cosmetics, which are often very dangerous for the health of citizens.
the recent terrorist attacks have brought to the attention of the public a need that is not new but one that is particularly important and urgent today. our attention must not only be directed to the perpetrators or potential perpetrators of the attacks in order to ensure an effective repressive and preventive response, but also to the victims, whether direct or indirect. the need to improve legislation and support measures for the protection of victims of crime, including, as a matter of priority, victims of terrorism, which naturally includes the family members of direct victims, was recognised in the 2009 stockholm programme. the directive 2012/29/eu on victims of crime also recognises that victims of terrorism, as they suffer the consequences of crimes against society as a whole, need special attention and that, now more than ever, victims of terrorism need to be able to rely on national and international solidarity and support. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to take them up in the next few months. free medical, psychological, social and material assistance must be provided immediately. long-term assistance is needed, both for those who have suffered physical or psychological damage directly as a result of terrorist acts and, where necessary, for their families. effective access to justice, including the possibility of legal assistance and adequate compensation and compensation for damage suffered, is needed and it is also important to recognise and support the role of victim protection associations.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the text in question refers to an agreement between the european police office europol and the united arab emirates on strategic cooperation in the fight against serious crime and terrorism. in view of the particularity of the present situation, we must support all efforts to prevent and combat criminal acts which threaten the personal and economic well-being of our citizens, and it is of the utmost importance to create the conditions for the perpetrators of these crimes to be brought to justice. the agreement under discussion today, which the council has informally approved pending consultation of the european parliament, will formally establish cooperation between the european union and the united arab emirates in the field of security and the fight against organised crime through the exchange of information on crime prevention methods, expertise and the results of strategic analysis. this agreement is strategic and not operational, so it excludes any implications for personal data and, as europol has repeatedly pointed out, the uae is becoming a hotbed for economic and financial crime. it is well known that they are considered a destination country for proceeds of illicit activities, such as vat fraud against european states, and money laundering. it is clear that more structured cooperation would strengthen europol's coordinating role with a view to concretely resolving investigations whose outcome involves two or more european states. cross-border criminal networks can only be effectively tackled through synergistic cooperation at international level. in the light of the above and taking into account the time limits for the european parliament to participate in the procedure provided for in this specific case, i have tabled a report supporting the council's decision to authorise the agreement negotiated between europol and the united arab emirates on the fight against crime and terrorism.

president of the eurogroup.– mr president, thank you for inviting me to this plenary session of parliament. it is the first time i have had the honour to be here. i find it quite intimidating. you, of course, are very much used to this arena, but to me it is still a new experience. it is a sincere pleasure for me to take part in today’s exchange of views on the euro area recommendation. i am sure president juncker will explain the commission’s proposal of 26 november. he is best placed for this, so i will not go into the details. as the eurogroup president, i support a timely discussion of the euro area recommendation which gives a more prominent role to the euro area dimension in the context of a revamped european semester. this fits into a necessary push towards a closer coordination of member states’ economic policies. one lesson learned from the crisis is that member states that are sharing a single currency need to be particularly mindful of the possible spillovers, both positive and negative, of their domestic policies. in that sense, i believe, broadly speaking, that the commission’s draft recommendation raises the right issues. the gradual economic recovery is ongoing and is relatively broadly based across member states. this shows that the work we have done together over the last couple of years is starting to pay off and bolster confidence. however, since we will not be able to count on several supportive factors, such as low oil prices and a very accommodative monetary policy, forever, we need to ensure that the recovery becomes self-sustained, in particular given the weaker external environment. therefore it is essential that policy agendas remain focused on investment, structural reforms and, obviously, sustainable and growth-friendly fiscal policies. this is needed to improve competitiveness, in particular by unlocking the euro area’s productive capacity, and thereby fostering higher sustainable and inclusive growth. it is the surest way to address the still unacceptably high unemployment rates and legacy debt in many countries. it is crucial if we want a thriving euro area in a globalised world, and it is also the only way to preserve our european social model. although the euro area recommendation and the country-specific recommendations by and large address the right issues, effective economic policy coordination requires attention for implementation at member state level. going forward, it will be important to regularly monitor the progress made in implementing the recommendations and enhancing national ownership. this is why the issues i have just mentioned have figured and will continue to figure prominently in the eurogroup’s work programme, notably in the context of our thematic discussions on growth and jobs. these discussions are a follow-up to the euro area recommendation, working on best practices and benchmarking, for example on the tax wedge on labour, or pension reforms. and this brings me to the so-called five presidents’ report on completing europe’s economic and monetary union, which the president of the european parliament and i co-authored, together with presidents juncker, tusk and draghi. the report pointed out that despite significant improvements in recent years, more work is needed to make the emu more resilient and its institutional architecture more complete in order to maximise the benefits of participating in the single currency to its members. we aimed to strike the right balance between realism and vision, which is reflected in a stage-based approach. until mid-2017 it proposes short-term measures to make the euro area more resilient, while making the best possible use of the current legal framework. these are intended to pave the way for more far-reaching measures for completing the emu in the second stage. pursuing convergence is a key theme in the report. over the last years, member states have made significant steps, but the smooth functioning of a monetary union requires further efforts to reduce divergence in economic and fiscal performance, financial market fragmentation, as well as differences in national institutional architecture. all these aspects are interlinked, and simultaneous progress is needed. it is indisputable in my mind that participation in a monetary union comes with the sharing of sovereignty. the key question is, however, how much sovereignty should be shared under which conditions. in other words, we need to be clear on what we want to achieve, and then determine how to go about it. the process of deepening the emu is indeed also about risk sharing, but in order to make progress on this front, member states need to make progress in further reducing risks. this entails repairing economic and fiscal imbalances through a consistent and faithful application of instruments like the stability and growth pact and the macroeconomic imbalance procedure. between risk reduction and risk sharing, we need to work on our economic risk absorption capacity. it will not surprise you that i am convinced that private risk sharing is as important as public risk sharing. the experience in the us has shown that integrated financial markets account for the largest part of the absorption of asymmetric economic shocks. developing the capital markets union, therefore, should be a priority. similarly, we need a comprehensive approach to completing the banking union in order to decisively break the vicious sovereign banking nexus. the key element in building the banking union was the paradigm shift from bail-out to bail-in. this is a fundamental shift in our approach, where risks will be pushed back to where they belong. but more needs to be done to strengthen the resilience of our banking system. for example, dealing with over 150 national options and discretions left to date, reducing sovereign risks, and applying the bail-in rules in full to ensure a level playing field. this is as important as decisive progress towards a european deposit insurance scheme or a credible backstop to the single resolution fund. the three will have to be brought forward together. it is essential that we join efforts to build dynamic, flexible and upward converging economies that are supported by a well-integrated financial market with private risk sharing and by sound public finances with fiscal buffers for difficult times. my plea for further integration at euro area level should go hand in hand with greater accountability, legitimacy and institutional strengthening. this affects national and european policy makers, as well as national parliaments and the european parliament. as far as the european parliament is concerned, i believe it should be able to fully exploit its prerogatives under the current treaties and secondary legislation when it comes to the european semester. the preparatory work for moving to the second stage of completing the emu should include a debate on the role and competences of the different institutional actors in a deep and genuine monetary union. the measures outlined in the five presidents’ report and the recent commission initiatives to operationalise them are given careful consideration in different fora. i will assume my responsibility and facilitate the non-legislative and legislative procedures, both from the perspective of the eurogroup presidency and of the next presidency of the ecofin council.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i believe that economic and monetary union has been strengthened by the last serious economic crisis compared to what we had in the past, but unfortunately it remains incomplete. despite the progress we have made and with regard to strengthening economic governance and even the launch of the banking union, we still have a lot to do. our efforts must be directed towards a union capable of achieving greater growth, employment and prosperity for all citizens, without any class distinction, but at the same time it must also be based on solid foundations to meet not only domestic but also global challenges. we must certainly be more competitive with the united states and china as well. i am aware that employment and social developments have been examined in detail in the country reports during the year, with country-specific recommendations, but i would like to stress the urgency and the need to improve the labour market and social performance, certainly to give confidence to all those young people who are still out of work and have a very high rate of youth unemployment. flexsecurity is certainly important, we need to have flexible, reliable employment contracts - not precarious employment, which is a totally different matter - favourable taxation of work, which of course facilitates new recruitment, lifelong learning programmes and job placement aid. i think that we must be more operational at this time, also from an employment point of view.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, president juncker has reminded us that we are experiencing a better structuring of institutional relations in view of the necessary reforms in the second phase of the five-chairman report. i think that there is a clear need for a better structuring of institutional relations, as this debate shows. i think the central point, which has emerged also from many critical debates and not just positive ones, is that we need more political responsibility and democratic legitimacy for the euro area and that we expect the commission to tell us quickly what it thinks can be done immediately within the lisbon treaty, within the existing treaties and what needs to be done by amending the treaties appropriately, if necessary. i think there are two economic points and one political point. the two economic points are: more investment is needed and therefore instruments are needed to bring euro area investment to at least the two trillion needed for the next few years. is an estimate made by the commission. the second is a social pact that defines social rules within a highly integrated area such as the euro area. on the institutional level, however, i believe that the debate should continue on the political relations between the commission and the european parliament, the european parliament and the national parliaments.
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, first of all, i would like to thank members for this fruitful debate. while different views and opinions were expressed, i draw comfort from the fairly broad agreement on the need to strengthen economic and monetary union (emu). completing the emu institutional framework is one of the key issues the eu is facing today, and i believe that the other major challenges which have emerged makes this task even more – not less – urgent. the commission has proposed concrete steps and we value very highly the debates we have held on these matters with parliament and the feedback we have received. as president juncker has stressed, the commission thinks that parliament has a key role to play in ensuring the democratic legitimacy and accountability of economic governance. we need to build on the stronger involvement of parliament, which has happened in recent years, for instance via the economic dialogue. the commissioners concerned and i will continue to be available for discussions on economic matters. we are already listening to members’ calls, for instance by giving more attention to the euro area dimension and to social considerations in the european semester. we must work together to fine tune the best way forward. i have also carefully taken note of members’ remarks on the euro area recommendation. the views of parliament on this recommendation are important and, in the commission’s view, they should feed into the finalisation of the recommendation as it goes through the council. let me conclude by saying that i look forward to continuing to work together during the 2016 european semester.
in writing. i would like to focus on two points. the first concerns investment, which is known to be held back in the euro area by at least three factors: weak demand dynamics, debt accumulation and weak private sector confidence. it is imperative that the eurozone, in addition to supporting demand, address the issue of debt and fragile confidence. the european central bank must put in place monetary policy measures that can actually help to support the economic recovery of the euro area. the second point concerns a proposal recently adopted by the college of european commissioners to revise the approach to the european semester and improve the economic governance of the euro area. the euro area member states should have a unified representation in the international financial institutions, in particular the international monetary fund. if each member state of the euro area speaks for itself, or worse if they contradict each other, the euro area will never have the weight that it should have to complete economic and monetary union. much depends on how it is implemented and whether the coordination mechanism is created to prepare the unified positions that the president of the eurogroup could and should present to the international monetary fund on behalf of all the member states of the euro area.
